weeks.title: The Triune God: Source of Relationship
weeks.theme: Relationships begin not with technique but with the triune God: we were made in love and we live for love.
group: Read John 17:20-23. What did Jesus ask for in his disciples’ relationships, and what did he hold up as the model?
What did you used to think “socializing” was for, and how has your view of relationships shifted this week?
Whom do you want to take the initiative to love this week? Name one concrete step and ask the group to pray for you—will you do that?
weeks.sunday: Invite a friend or neighbor you haven’t been in touch with for a long time to share a cup of tea or a simple meal. Before you head out, pray: “Lord, let me be like you today—let me love first.” While you’re together, ask more, listen more, and talk about yourself less. When you get home, write down a one-line prayer for that person, and thank God for letting you taste his love through your time together.

lessons.title: One in Us
lessons.hear:
On the night he was betrayed, on his way to the cross, Jesus prayed for his disciples—and for everyone who would one day believe in him. He didn’t ask for their success or for a trouble-free life. He asked for relationship: “that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us” (John 17:21).

Notice the model Jesus uses. It isn’t a happy family or a team with perfect chemistry. It is the relationship between the Father and the Son. Jesus goes on: “you loved me before the foundation of the world” (John 17:24). Before there were stars, before there were people, the deepest reality in the universe was already love: the Father loving the Son, the Son answering the Father, and the Spirit flowing between them. God was never sitting alone on a throne waiting for someone to keep him company. He himself is an eternal fellowship of love.

That changes how we see our social lives. The world says relationships are a skill—networking, building connections, getting ahead. But Scripture says the source of every relationship is in God. Every sincere love between two people is an echo of the love within the Trinity. Think of a piece of music: the melody lives first in the composer’s heart, and only then can the orchestra play it. Because the fellowship of love was first in God’s heart, we are able to love one another.

So learning to live well with others doesn’t start with communication techniques. It starts by going back to the source. Ask the Holy Spirit to open your eyes to see that you have been invited into the love of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit. When we live in that love, our relationships with others finally have roots.
lessons.light: Relationships have an order: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, then with tasks. The first step in our social life isn’t “Whom should I get to know?” but “Whose love am I living in?” Moving from a human point of view to God’s point of view: relationships aren’t tools; they reflect God’s own nature. To let Jesus reign begins by letting his love become the source of every relationship I have.
think: In John 17:21-23, what does Jesus compare his disciples’ unity to?
In my relationships, do I tend to treat people as tools to be managed, or as an overflow of love?
How can I let one relationship reflect God’s love today?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that before the foundation of the world you shared love with the Son, and that you have invited me into that love. Forgive me for so often treating relationships as techniques and tools. Holy Spirit, help me first remain in your love, and then love the people around me out of that love, so that others may come to know you through the way we love one another. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Copy John 17:21 into the notes app on your phone today. Tonight before bed, think of one person in your life and pray for them for one minute, asking God to let your relationship reflect his love.
lessons.quick: At the very heart of the universe is not loneliness but the love of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit.
text: “Not for these only do I pray, but for those also who will believe in me through their word,
that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.
The glory which you have given me, I have given to them, that they may be one, even as we are one,
I in them, and you in me, that they may be perfected into one, that the world may know that you sent me and loved them, even as you loved me.
Father, I desire that they also whom you have given me be with me where I am, that they may see my glory which you have given me, for you loved me before the foundation of the world.
Righteous Father, the world hasn’t known you, but I knew you; and these knew that you sent me.
I made known to them your name, and will make it known; that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.”

lessons.title: Made in God’s Image for Relationship
lessons.hear:
A young brother who worked at a tech company described his life as highly efficient: computer at work, phone after work, binge-watching alone on weekends. “Relationships are too much hassle,” he said. “I do just fine on my own.” Then he came down with a bad flu and lay for three days in his small rented room. He had hundreds of contacts in his phone, yet couldn’t think of a single person he could ask to bring him a bowl of soup.

Many of us carry an old mindset: people are basically independent individuals, and relationships are an optional extra—something to invest in when we have time and drop when we don’t. God sees it very differently. Genesis says, “Let’s make man in our image, after our likeness” (Genesis 1:26). Notice that God says “our.” Many of the church fathers saw here a glimpse of the Trinity: a God who lives in loving fellowship made humanity after his own likeness. Then the text says, “God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). From the moment humanity was created, it was plural—it existed in relationship.

This means relationships aren’t an add-on to life; they are what we were made to be. Just as fish are made for water and birds for the sky, people are made to love and to be loved. When someone shuts themselves away, they aren’t “freer”—they have left their proper place as creatures. It’s like putting a fish on dry land: it looks calm, but it is actually suffocating.

After that brother recovered, he started attending a small group at church. He wasn’t much of a talker, so he volunteered to bring the drinks. Six months later he said, “It turns out I didn’t not need people—I just thought I didn’t.” That is God’s grace: he made us in his image, and step by step he brings us back into relationship.
lessons.light: Moving from a human point of view to God’s point of view: people don’t just “have” relationships—we are made for relationship. The self-centered life wants to be independent, self-sufficient, and its own king. The selfless life admits: I need God, and I need people. Returning to our proper place means returning to the relationships God designed when he made us in his image.
think: In Genesis 1:26-27, what do “our” and “male and female” reveal?
Have I ever thought I was “doing just fine on my own” and didn’t need anyone else?
Whom can I tell “I need you” this week, so that the relationship becomes more real?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for making me in your image, able to love and to be loved. I confess that sometimes I shut myself away and think I don’t need anyone. Heal the defensiveness in my heart, bring me back into the relationships you designed, and make me someone others can lean on. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, send a message to someone you rarely reach out to—a family member, an old classmate, or a coworker—and thank them specifically for one way they once helped you.
lessons.quick: We don’t just have relationships; we were made for them.
text: God said, “Let’s make man in our image, after our likeness. Let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.”
God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”

lessons.title: Love Comes from God
lessons.hear:
When John wrote this letter, he was already an aged apostle. Tradition says that late in life he would be carried into the gathering and would say only one thing, over and over: “Little children, love one another.” Whether or not that story is entirely accurate, John’s letters certainly speak of love in a way that is both utterly simple and utterly profound: “He who doesn’t love doesn’t know God, for God is love” (1 John 4:8).

John doesn’t say God has love; he says God is love. Love isn’t one of God’s hobbies—it is his very nature. And this love doesn’t stay in the realm of theory; it acts: “God has sent his only born Son into the world that we might live through him” (1 John 4:9). The love of the triune God pours outward—onto the cross and into our hearts.

Then John says something astonishing: “No one has seen God at any time. If we love one another, God remains in us” (1 John 4:12). The world can’t see God. But people can see how a Christian treats the neighbors, replies to messages in the group chat, and speaks to a harried server at a restaurant. Our love for one another becomes the visible face of the invisible God.

So today’s practice is simple: let God’s love flow through you to one real person. It doesn’t have to be dramatic. Just be like a pipe—a pipe doesn’t have to produce water; it only has to stay open and unclogged. Maybe you thank the coworker who always orders lunch for everyone. Maybe you spend ten minutes chatting with an elderly neighbor who lives alone. Maybe you post a warm reply in the group chat for someone who has been overlooked. Love comes from God; all you have to do is let it flow.
lessons.light: Rely on the Holy Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head. Love isn’t squeezed out by willpower; it flows out of God. The “2” in 920 stands for every person connected to me. Choose one “2” today and let the life of Christ flow through you to them. A pipe doesn’t need to be proud or ashamed; as long as it stays open, the water naturally reaches where it needs to go.
think: In 1 John 4:9-10, how was God’s love revealed?
Is my love more like a reservoir (it only stores) or a pipe (it flows)?
To whom will I let God’s love flow today, and how?
lessons.speak: Father, you are love, and you sent your only Son so that I might live. Make me an open pipe—not clogged, not holding back—so that today I carry your love to one real person. Let people see what you are like through the way we love one another. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Before noon today, decide on one person: an often-overlooked coworker, a neighbor, or an older person. Sometime today, reach out and greet them, and do one small thing for them—help with something, keep them company, or bring them a drink.
lessons.quick: The world can’t see God, but it can see how we love one another.
text: Beloved, let’s love one another, for love is of God; and everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God.
He who doesn’t love doesn’t know God, for God is love.
By this God’s love was revealed in us, that God has sent his only born Son into the world that we might live through him.
In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
Beloved, if God loved us in this way, we also ought to love one another.
No one has seen God at any time. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love has been perfected in us.

lessons.title: Babel-Style Socializing
lessons.hear:
Humanity’s first large-scale “team project” was the tower of Babel. The people had a common language, a common goal, and common technology. They looked remarkably united. But they said, “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves” (Genesis 11:4). Their unity wasn’t for God but for their own name. They weren’t building each other up; they were using each other so they could be seen.

So God confused their language. They could no longer understand one another, and they scattered. Connections centered on ourselves may look tight on the outside, but inside they are fragile. Many social circles today are just like Babel: people stick together because they are useful to each other, and once the benefit is gone, the group falls apart.

Let this passage hold up a mirror. When I go to gatherings, join group chats, or keep up certain relationships, is it out of love, or to “make a name” for myself? Do I only spend time with people who can help me? When I’m with others, am I building them up, or building my own tower? These questions aren’t meant to condemn us; they let the Holy Spirit point out where we are self-centered.

The good news is that the story doesn’t end at Babel. At Pentecost the Holy Spirit came, and “everyone heard them speaking in his own language” (Acts 2:6). Babel scattered people because of self-centeredness; Pentecost united them by the Spirit. The way to adjust isn’t to work harder at networking. It is to lay down our own towers and let the Holy Spirit join us together again. Today, confess to God one place where you have been “building a tower for yourself” in a relationship, and hand it over to him.
lessons.light: Self-centeredness is the root of humanity’s fall and the root of every broken relationship. Babel wanted to “make a name for ourselves,” but the fellowship of the Trinity is all about honoring one another. When we let Jesus receive all the glory, our relationships are no longer about building towers for ourselves; together we build God’s system. Tearing down our own tower isn’t a loss—it is how we gain true companions.
think: In Genesis 11:4, what motivated the people to build the tower?
Is there a relationship in which I am actually building a “tower” for myself?
How will I hand the motives behind that relationship back to God?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that I often build towers for myself among people—wanting to be seen and affirmed, and spending time only with those who are useful to me. Forgive me, and tear down the Babel in my heart. Holy Spirit, let my relationships no longer be for my name but for yours. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of someone you have drifted away from because they “weren’t much use”—a retired senior colleague, perhaps, or a socially awkward classmate. Send them a friendly message today with no agenda at all.
lessons.quick: Connections centered on ourselves look tight but are actually fragile.
text: The whole earth was of one language and of one speech.
As they traveled east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and they lived there.
They said to one another, “Come, let’s make bricks, and burn them thoroughly.” They had brick for stone, and they used tar for mortar.
They said, “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth.”
The LORD came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of men built.
The LORD said, “Behold, they are one people, and they all have one language, and this is what they begin to do. Now nothing will be withheld from them, which they intend to do.
Come, let’s go down, and there confuse their language, that they may not understand one another’s speech.”
So the LORD scattered them abroad from there on the surface of all the earth. They stopped building the city.
Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the LORD confused the language of all the earth. From there, the LORD scattered them abroad on the surface of all the earth.

lessons.title: Keeping the Unity of the Spirit
lessons.hear:
This week we went back to the source of relationship. We saw Jesus praying that his disciples would be one as the Father and the Son are one. We saw that people were made in God’s image and created for relationship. We learned to let God’s love flow through us like water, and we held up a mirror to the Babel in our own hearts. Now it’s time to make what we’ve received stick—and to pass it on.

Paul urges the church in Ephesians to be “eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:3). Notice that unity is “of the Spirit”—it is given, not manufactured by us—yet we must be eager to keep it. It’s as if God has given us a garden: he planted the flowers, but weeding and watering are our job. Paul continues: “one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in us all” (Ephesians 4:6). The triune God isn’t only the model for our relationships; he lives among us and personally binds us together.

How do we keep that unity? Paul gives us a list: “with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love” (Ephesians 4:2). None of these are advanced techniques. They are the life that appears when the self dies and Christ lives in us—and that is what we will practice, bit by bit, throughout this whole year.

Repetition means reminding yourself every morning: “I am loved by the love of the triune God.” Multiplication means telling one person, in your own words, what you learned this week. It could be someone in your small group, your child, your roommate, or a friend who is exploring the faith. Tell them, “We weren’t made for loneliness. We were made for love.”
lessons.light: Change your mindset and you change your life. This week’s new mindset: the source of relationship is the triune God. “Multiplication” in the eight steps means passing on what we have received. The “2” in 235 reminds us that faith isn’t a solo journey—find a companion to walk with you. Love never shrinks as it is shared; the more it is given away, the more it grows.
think: According to Ephesians 4:2-3, what qualities of character does keeping unity require?
Which truth touched me most this week, and why?
With whom will I share what I received this week, and when?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for bringing me back to the source of relationship this week. Holy Spirit, help me be eager to keep the unity you give—living out humility, gentleness, and patience in my family, my church, and among my friends. And give me the courage to tell someone about your love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, connect with a brother or sister in person or by phone. Take three minutes to share the verse that touched you most this week, invite them to share too, and then pray for each other.
lessons.quick: Unity is the Spirit’s gift; our job is to be eager to keep it.
text: I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called,
with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love,
being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
There is one body and one Spirit, even as you also were called in one hope of your calling,
one Lord, one faith, one baptism,
one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in us all.

weeks.title: Not Good to Be Alone
weeks.theme: Loneliness is more than a feeling—it is a drift from how we were made, and God himself places us in relationship.
group: Read Genesis 2:18-20. Amid everything God called “good,” why did he say something was “not good”?
When have you felt the loneliest, and what got you through that time?
Who around you this week might be on their own, and how are you willing to walk alongside them for a while?
weeks.sunday: Find someone who lives alone, has just moved to the area, or has recently arrived from overseas, and invite them for a meal or to drop by your home (use good judgment about boundaries; feel free to bring a third person along). Before you go, pray: “Lord, you set the lonely in families—please use me.” Afterward, thank God for that person, and note one need they mentioned so you can follow up next week.

lessons.title: The First Time God Said “Not Good”
lessons.hear:
Genesis 1 reads like a majestic poem. Each time God finished a day’s work, he saw that it was good. Light was good. Sea and land were good. Plants and trees, birds and beasts—all good. Then, in chapter 2, we hear God say “not good” for the first time: “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him” (Genesis 2:18).

That is astonishing. At this point Adam had no sin. He lived in a perfect garden, walked with God every day, had meaningful work, and lacked nothing to eat or drink. By our reckoning he had everything. Yet God said: not good. Even with God’s presence, meaningful work, and a beautiful world, humans were still made for relationship with one another. Then God brought the animals to Adam to name, and the text says, “but for man there was not found a helper comparable to him” (Genesis 2:20). It is as if God let Adam discover for himself that among all creatures, not one could meet him face to face and heart to heart.

This passage speaks directly about marriage, but behind it lies a larger principle: people were not made to be alone. Single people are not incomplete—Jesus himself never married. But every one of us, married or single, needs family, friends, and spiritual companions. Loneliness isn’t proof of weakness. It is the way we were made sending out a signal, just as thirst tells the body it needs water.

More beautiful still, God didn’t just notice what was “not good”; he took action himself. It was God who placed the man in relationship, and God who brought the woman to him. Today he is still the God who prepares companions for the lonely.
lessons.light: Loneliness at its root is a drift from our proper place as creatures. God is the designer of relationship, yet we often want to be our own king, protecting ourselves with independence and self-sufficiency. Returning to our proper place means admitting: God made me to need him, and to need people. That isn’t weakness; it’s humility—letting God be God and letting others into my life.
think: In Genesis 2:18-20, how did God help Adam realize his need?
Do I see “needing other people” as a kind of weakness?
How can I admit my relational needs to God today?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for seeing human loneliness and stepping in yourself. You know there are places in my heart no one has ever really entered. Heal my self-protection, bring me into the relationships you have prepared for me, and make me a companion for others too. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Take five minutes today to list three people you can honestly share your heart with. If you can’t think of even one, tell God about that need specifically and ask him to provide a companion for you.
lessons.quick: In a perfect paradise, God said: it is not good for the man to be alone.
text: The LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.
The LORD God commanded the man, saying, “You may freely eat of every tree of the garden;
but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.”
The LORD God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.”

Out of the ground the LORD God formed every animal of the field, and every bird of the sky, and brought them to the man to see what he would call them. Whatever the man called every living creature became its name.
The man gave names to all livestock, and to the birds of the sky, and to every animal of the field; but for man there was not found a helper comparable to him.
The LORD God caused the man to fall into a deep sleep. As the man slept, he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh in its place.
The LORD God made a woman from the rib which he had taken from the man, and brought her to the man.
The man said, “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. She will be called ‘woman,’ because she was taken out of Man.”
Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.
The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.

lessons.title: Two Are Better Than One
lessons.hear:
A brother in his fifties had spent his younger years building his career, moving from city to city and doing well in business. After retiring, he moved to Singapore to live with his children. They were at work all day, so he spent his days sitting at the foot of his apartment block, watching people come and go. “I used to be too busy to make friends,” he said. “Now I have the time, but I don’t know where to find any.”

Ecclesiastes described this kind of person long ago: “There is one who is alone, and he has neither son nor brother. There is no end to all of his labor … ‘For whom then do I labor and deprive my soul of enjoyment?’” (Ecclesiastes 4:8). Our old mindset often says: take care of your career first, relationships can wait; relying on yourself is safest, because people will always let you down. But the Teacher states God’s view in the most practical terms: “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor” (Ecclesiastes 4:9). When you fall, someone helps you up. When it’s cold, you keep each other warm. When you’re attacked, someone stands beside you. And the last line goes deeper still: “a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecclesiastes 4:12). Many pastors read the third strand as God himself: when God is at the center of a friendship between two people, it becomes all the stronger.

That brother was eventually invited by a retired neighbor to the church’s seniors’ fellowship. At first he only came to play chess. Later he began giving rides to older folks who had trouble getting around. “It turns out,” he said, “that being needed brings you more alive than making money ever did.”

Loneliness can run very deep. If it troubles you for a long time and affects your sleep and daily life, seeking counseling or medical help is also God’s grace. Whatever you do, don’t carry it alone. The strand of cord God has prepared for you may be living just downstairs.
lessons.light: The self-centered life says, “Relying on myself is safest.” The selfless life says, “I need you, and you need me.” People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Change your mindset and you change your living: no longer putting relationships last, but restoring them to God’s designed order—first God, then people, and only then tasks.
think: What benefits of companionship does Ecclesiastes 4:9-12 list?
Have I also put relationships behind my career or my busyness?
For which lonely person could I become that “second strand”?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that I often want to rely on myself. I’m afraid of troubling others and afraid of being rejected. Thank you for saying that two are better than one. Give me courage to reach out, and the willingness to let others help me up. Be the third strand in our relationships. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, reach out to someone you know is fairly lonely—an older person, a coworker from out of town, or a new friend—and set a specific time this week to share a meal or take a walk together.
lessons.quick: Two are better than one—and with God at the center, the cord is not quickly broken.
text: Then I returned and saw vanity under the sun.

There is one who is alone, and he has neither son nor brother. There is no end to all of his labor, neither are his eyes satisfied with wealth. “For whom then do I labor and deprive my soul of enjoyment?” This also is vanity. Yes, it is a miserable business.
Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.
Again, if two lie together, then they have warmth; but how can one keep warm alone?
If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

lessons.title: God Sets the Lonely in Families
lessons.hear:
Psalm 68 is a victory song. It pictures God as a conquering king riding through the wilderness. But in the middle of this grand scene, the psalmist suddenly zooms in to show us what this great King is doing: “A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in his holy habitation. God sets the lonely in families” (Psalm 68:5-6).

What a tender God! He rules the universe, yet he notices the people nobody notices: children who have lost their parents, widows who have lost their husbands, people living alone far from home. And how does God set the lonely in families? In Scripture, God usually doesn’t drop a family down from heaven. He opens doors through his people. The church is the family God has prepared for the lonely—and you and I are the ones assigned to open the door.

Today, think about the “lonely ones” in your circle. Maybe it’s a student who just came from Malaysia to study in Taipei. Maybe it’s a new coworker who always eats lunch alone. Maybe it’s an older woman in your neighborhood whose husband recently passed away. Or maybe it’s the friend who posted in the group chat and got no reply. They may never say, “I’m lonely,” but an invitation or a simple greeting could be a door God is opening for them.

Act with wisdom. Be careful about spending time alone with someone of the opposite sex, and when you invite someone you don’t know well into your home, include family members or people from your small group. Love isn’t reckless; it’s considerate. You don’t have to become everything to someone. You only need to be a key in God’s hand, so that a lonely person knows: in God’s family, there is a seat saved for them.
lessons.light: The “2” in 920 is every person connected to me. God often places lonely people at the edges of our circles, waiting for us to notice them. To let Jesus reign is to let his heart become mine: he notices orphans and widows, so I learn to notice the overlooked. This is the most ordinary and most beautiful step in building God’s system.
think: In Psalm 68:5-6, what does God do, and for whom?
Who in my circle might be one of “the lonely”?
How will I open a door for them today?
lessons.speak: Father, you are a father of the fatherless and a defender of widows, and you set the lonely in families. Open my eyes to see the overlooked people around me, and open my heart to welcome them into my home and my life. Use me as a key in your hand. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, find someone who often eats alone or has just arrived somewhere unfamiliar, and invite them to lunch or coffee. If meeting in person isn’t possible, call them and chat for ten minutes.
lessons.quick: God sets the lonely in families—and we are the ones who open the door.
text: Sing to God! Sing praises to his name! Extol him who rides on the clouds: to the LORD, his name! Rejoice before him!
A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in his holy habitation.
God sets the lonely in families. He brings out the prisoners with singing, but the rebellious dwell in a sun-scorched land.

lessons.title: Only Luke Is with Me
lessons.hear:
Over his lifetime Paul led countless people to faith and planted many churches. Yet in his very last letter we hear the voice of a lonely old man: “Demas left me, having loved this present world” (2 Timothy 4:10); “At my first defense, no one came to help me, but all left me” (2 Timothy 4:16). Even the great apostle knew what it was to be abandoned by friends.

This passage is a mirror that shows us two things. First, have I ever been like Demas? When a friend lost a job, fell ill, was misunderstood, or got into trouble, did I quietly leave the group chat and stop replying to their messages? We usually don’t abandon people on purpose. We’re just “too busy,” or we “don’t know what to say,” or we’re afraid of getting caught up in the mess. Second, when others left, was I like Luke? Paul writes, “Only Luke is with me” (2 Timothy 4:11). Luke didn’t leave behind any earth-shaking exploits. He simply stayed.

This passage also hides a story of restoration. Paul says, “Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service” (2 Timothy 4:11). Years earlier, Mark had left in the middle of a missionary journey, and Paul refused to take him along again (see Acts 15:37-38). Now Paul himself asks for him to come back. People who once left can be restored; people who once rejected others can welcome them again.

Deeper still is Paul’s testimony: “But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me” (2 Timothy 4:17). When everyone else left, the Lord did not. Today, ask the Lord to show you someone you have drifted away from—and ask him to make you a Luke, someone willing to stay.
lessons.light: Self-centered relationships say, “I’ll come when you’re useful and leave when there’s trouble.” Selfless love stays when others hit rock bottom. Relationships matter more than tasks, and being present matters more than fixing things. Paul and Mark’s restoration reminds us that the “relationships” part of the five-fold change often requires one side to let go of old judgments and the other to be willing to come back.
think: In 2 Timothy 4:9-18, who left Paul, who stayed, and what did the Lord do?
When my friends hit rock bottom, am I more like Demas or like Luke?
How will I reconnect with a friend I have drifted away from?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you never abandon me; when everyone leaves, you still stand by me. Forgive me for stepping back when my friends needed me. Give me Luke’s faithfulness to stay with others in their low points, and Paul’s generous heart to welcome back those who once let me down. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of a friend who is going through a hard time and whom you haven’t contacted in a while. Send them a message today: “I’ve been thinking of you lately. How are you doing? Is there anything I can pray for?”
lessons.quick: Love doesn’t always mean doing something big; sometimes it simply means staying.
text: Be diligent to come to me soon,
for Demas left me, having loved this present world, and went to Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia; and Titus to Dalmatia.
Only Luke is with me. Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service.
But I sent Tychicus to Ephesus.
Bring the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus when you come—and the books, especially the parchments.
Alexander the coppersmith did much evil to me. The Lord will repay him according to his deeds.
Beware of him, for he greatly opposed our words.
At my first defense, no one came to help me, but all left me. May it not be held against them.
But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, that through me the message might be fully proclaimed, and that all the Gentiles might hear. So I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion.
And the Lord will deliver me from every evil work and will preserve me for his heavenly Kingdom. To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.

lessons.title: A Family That Shares Life
lessons.hear:
This week we heard God say, “It is not good for the man to be alone.” We saw that two are better than one, learned to open the door for lonely people, and examined whether we have ever walked away from friends the way Demas did. Now let’s look at God’s answer for a lonely world: a family that belongs to him.

After Pentecost, the early church was born. Luke describes their life like this: “They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer” (Acts 2:42). Fellowship means sharing life together. They didn’t just gather on the weekend. “Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart” (Acts 2:46). Among them were local Jews, Jews who had come back from distant lands, rich and poor—people who had been strangers to one another, yet in Christ they became one family.

Notice that the center of this family wasn’t a program but a dinner table and prayer. God sets the lonely in families, often through a table, a shared loaf of bread, a simple “Come eat with us.” The same is true for the church today: a small group, a fellowship, a home-cooked meal can all become a family for the lonely.

Repetition means reminding yourself every day: I am not an orphan; I belong to God’s family. Multiplication means opening the door of that family a little wider. This weekend you could invite someone to your small group or to your table, or ask a spiritual companion to pray with you for the lonely people around you. That’s how a family grows—one invitation at a time.
lessons.light: The “2” in 235 stands for spiritual companions: don’t walk the road of faith alone. The order of change is life first, then relationships, then ministry. The early church’s influence didn’t begin with programs; it began with lives shared in fellowship. Building God’s system often starts at a dinner table—and your table can be an outpost of God’s kingdom.
think: According to Acts 2:42-47, what marked the life of the early church?
Do I already have family in my church with whom I truly share life?
Whom can I invite to my small group or my table this week?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that in Christ I am no longer an orphan but a member of your household. Make our small group and our church like the early church, sharing life and gathering with gladness and sincere hearts. Use me to open the door of this family to lonely people. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, invite a friend who isn’t part of any small group to join yours or to share a meal. Also ask a spiritual companion to pray with you for that friend for five minutes.
lessons.quick: God sets the lonely in families, and that family often begins at a dinner table.

All who believed were together, and had all things in common.
They sold their possessions and goods, and distributed them to all, according as anyone had need.
Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart,

weeks.title: How Sin Tears Relationships Apart
weeks.theme: Sin first cuts us off from God, then brings hiding, blaming, and envy; the self-centered life is the root of every relational rift.
group: Read Genesis 3:8-13. What three things did Adam and Eve do before God?
In your own conflicts, which do you fall back on most often—hiding, blaming, or comparing?
Is there a relationship this week in which you are willing to own your part first? What is one step you will take?
weeks.sunday: Share a meal with your family or roommates. Before eating, have each person name one small thing they “could have done better this week.” No explanations needed—just say “I’m sorry” or “Thank you for bearing with me.” Pray for one another before the meal, and afterward thank God together: just as he called to Adam in the garden, he calls us today to come out of hiding.

lessons.title: From Hiding to Blaming
lessons.hear:
Genesis 3 is the scene of humanity’s first relational accident. It all begins with a question: “Has God really said …?” (Genesis 3:1). The serpent didn’t tell them outright to rebel. He simply got them to doubt God’s goodness. Then he made his fatal promise: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). Eating the fruit wasn’t mere appetite. It was a desire to leave humanity’s proper place, take God’s place, and decide for ourselves what is good and what is evil.

Watch the chain reaction sin set off. First, the relationship between people and God was broken: “the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden” (Genesis 3:8). Second, their relationship with themselves was distorted: they realized they were naked and began to feel shame and to cover up. Third, the relationship between people fell apart. When God questioned Adam, he said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it” (Genesis 3:12). The husband who had only recently said, “This is now bone of my bones,” now pushed his wife forward as a shield—and even quietly blamed God: it was this woman you gave me. Eve, in turn, blamed the serpent.

This is what sin looks like: first we leave God, then we hide, cover up, and shift the blame. Many of the conflicts we see today—at the office, in the family group chat, in a church small group—are, at their root, a rerun of the script from that garden.

But don’t miss this line: “The LORD God called to the man, and said to him, ‘Where are you?’” (Genesis 3:9). God knew exactly where Adam was. He was inviting him to come out. Where people hide, God comes looking. That is where all reconciliation begins.
lessons.light: Self-centeredness is the root of humanity’s fall: people wanted to be “like God,” to be their own lord and king. Pride means leaving our proper place and grasping power. Once our relationship with God is broken, our relationships with others crack as well. Relationships run in order—first with God, then with others—and sin destroys them in the same order. Repair, too, begins by coming back before God.
think: In Genesis 3:8-13, what relationships did sin break?
In conflict, what is my favorite version of “It’s all because he …”?
When God asks me today, “Where are you?” how will I answer honestly?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that I am often like Adam—hiding from you and blaming others. Thank you for not giving up on me but still calling, “Where are you?” Today I want to come out and face my sin honestly. Begin your healing in my relationship with you, and heal my relationships with others too. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, recall your most recent friction with someone. Write down the sentence you used to “push it onto them,” then rewrite it as a sentence that owns your responsibility, and hand it to God in prayer.
lessons.quick: Sin’s script: leave God, hide, blame. Grace’s script: God comes looking.
text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?”
The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden,
but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it. You shall not touch it, lest you die.’”
The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t really die,
for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.
Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves.
They heard the LORD God’s voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden.
The LORD God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?”
The man said, “I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid myself.”
God said, “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?”
The man said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.”
The LORD God said to the woman, “What have you done?” The woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”

lessons.title: Biting and Devouring One Another
lessons.hear:
After their father died, three siblings began quarreling over the old family house. The eldest brother said that as the firstborn he deserved a bigger share. The sister said she was the one who had cared for their father all those years. The middle brother only wanted to “follow the law.” At first it was just reminders in the family group chat. Then came screenshots, dredging up old grievances, even arguments over who had been the favorite as a child. A year later the house still hadn’t been divided, and the three families no longer sat at the same table for Lunar New Year dinner.

Our old mindset often says that fights happen because there’s something to divide, and if we just divide it fairly, there will be peace. Paul paints a much uglier picture: “But if you bite and devour one another, be careful that you don’t consume one another” (Galatians 5:15). Like wild animals trapped together, you take a bite out of me and I tear a chunk out of you, until there are no winners—only scars. The house still stands, but the family is gone.

Paul goes on to dig out the root. He lists “the works of the flesh,” and more than half of them are diseases of relationship: “hatred, strife, jealousies, outbursts of anger, rivalries, divisions” (Galatians 5:20), and also “envy” (Galatians 5:21). This matches James’s diagnosis: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” (James 4:1). The house was only the spark. What really caught fire was the “me” inside that wanted to be seen, to be compensated, to win.

God’s view opens another way: “For you, brothers, were called for freedom. Only don’t use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love be servants to one another” (Galatians 5:13). The way out isn’t trying harder to suppress it, but to “walk by the Spirit” (Galatians 5:16). After a time of prayer, the eldest brother eventually called his siblings: “Let’s have a professional divide the house properly, according to the rules—but I don’t want to lose you over a house.” The legal matters were handled as they should be, but first their hearts put down the knife. That winter, at the solstice festival, the three families sat at the same table again.
lessons.light: A self-centered heart turns relationships into battlefields: I want the bigger share, I want to be affirmed, I want the last word—and we end up biting and devouring until everyone loses. Selflessness doesn’t mean wanting nothing; it means letting Jesus reign and walking by the Spirit. Relationships run in order—first with God, then with others. When my heart is satisfied in God first, I no longer need to bite a piece out of my brother.
think: Among the works of the flesh in Galatians 5:19-21, which directly harm relationships?
In a relationship that’s currently strained, what do I most want to get?
What act of “through love be servants to one another” can I choose today instead of taking another bite?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that I bite and devour too—for my pride, for fairness, for compensation—wounding the people I love with my words. Holy Spirit, lead me, so that I don’t give the flesh an opportunity but serve others in love. Give me wisdom to say clearly what needs to be said, and help me let go of what my heart needs to release. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, identify a relationship that’s currently strained and stop responding in the group chat. Privately send the other person a message: “We can work through this slowly, but I really value you.”
lessons.quick: Biting and devouring has no winners; only walking by the Spirit leads off the battlefield.
text: For you, brothers, were called for freedom. Only don’t use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love be servants to one another.
For the whole law is fulfilled in one word, in this: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
But if you bite and devour one another, be careful that you don’t consume one another.
But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.
For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary to one another, that you may not do the things that you desire.
But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.
Now the deeds of the flesh are obvious, which are: adultery, sexual immorality, uncleanness, lustfulness,
idolatry, sorcery, hatred, strife, jealousies, outbursts of anger, rivalries, divisions, heresies,
envy, murders, drunkenness, orgies, and things like these; of which I forewarn you, even as I also forewarned you, that those who practice such things will not inherit God’s Kingdom.

lessons.title: I Am My Brother’s Keeper
lessons.hear:
When sin walked out of the garden, the first to be hurt was family. Cain and Abel were brothers who both brought offerings. God accepted Abel’s offering, “but he didn’t respect Cain and his offering. Cain was very angry, and the expression on his face fell” (Genesis 4:5). This is envy in its earliest form: someone else is blessed, and I feel something has been taken from me.

God didn’t punish Cain right away. Instead he gently warned him: “If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it” (Genesis 4:7). Sin is like a wild animal crouching at the door, waiting to pounce. But Cain didn’t listen. He lured his brother into the field and killed him. When God asked him where his brother was, he answered coldly, “I don’t know. Am I my brother’s keeper?” (Genesis 4:9).

That line is the manifesto of self-centered social life: his business has nothing to do with me; I only look after myself. Today it comes in new wording: “That’s his own choice.” “I’m not responsible for him.” “I saw the message—no need to reply.” But God’s answer is clear: yes, you are your brother’s keeper.

Today’s practice has two steps. First, rule over the sin crouching at your door. Think of someone you secretly envy or compare yourself with, thank God for the good things in their life, and bless them sincerely. Second, become a keeper. Think of someone you know is struggling but whom everyone has overlooked, and reach out to them. It could be a greeting, some time together, or practical help. Envy made Cain raise his fist; love moves us to open our hands.
lessons.light: The self-centered person says, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” The selfless person says, “Lord, you placed him beside me; I’m willing to look after him.” The “2” in 920 reminds me that every person connected to me has been entrusted to me by God. Envy is the fruit of the self-centered life, and blessing others is the best way to rule over it.
think: In Genesis 4:6-7, how did God warn Cain?
Is there someone I secretly compare myself with or envy?
Whose “keeper” will I be today, and how?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that I have Cain’s heart too: my face falls when I see others blessed, and I often say, “That’s none of my business.” Help me rule over the sin crouching at my door and sincerely give thanks for the good things in others’ lives. And make me a keeper of my brothers and sisters. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Do two things today: pray for someone you secretly compare yourself with and send them a sincere word of congratulations; then check in on a friend who is struggling and ask, “How have you been? Would it help if I spent some time with you?”
lessons.quick: I am my brother’s keeper: rule over envy and open your hands.
text: As time passed, Cain brought an offering to the LORD from the fruit of the ground.
Abel also brought some of the firstborn of his flock and of its fat. The LORD respected Abel and his offering,
but he didn’t respect Cain and his offering. Cain was very angry, and the expression on his face fell.
The LORD said to Cain, “Why are you angry? Why has the expression of your face fallen?
If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.”
Cain said to Abel, his brother, “Let’s go into the field.” While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him.
The LORD said to Cain, “Where is Abel, your brother?” He said, “I don’t know. Am I my brother’s keeper?”
The LORD said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground.

lessons.title: You Are the Man
lessons.hear:
David was a man after God’s own heart, yet he committed a terrible sin. He took Uriah’s wife and then had Uriah killed by another’s hand. That sin didn’t only offend God; it tore apart many relationships—the life of a loyal soldier, a family, and an entire army’s trust in its king. Worse still, David kept it all covered up for nearly a year while everything looked normal on the surface.

God sent the prophet Nathan to him. Nathan didn’t accuse him directly. Instead he told the story of a rich man who seized a poor man’s little lamb. David was furious: “the man who has done this deserves to die!” (2 Samuel 12:5). We’re all like that—we see other people’s sin clearly and our own only dimly. Then Nathan spoke the words that pierced him to the heart: “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7).

That is today’s mirror for review. When I criticize someone’s selfishness in a group chat, am I the same way? When I silently condemn a coworker for taking credit, have I ever done the same thing? Jesus said that we often see the speck in our brother’s eye but don’t consider the beam in our own (see Matthew 7:3).

David’s response is what set him most apart from Saul. He didn’t shift the blame or make excuses. He simply said, “I have sinned against the LORD” (2 Samuel 12:13). Nathan replied at once: “The LORD also has put away your sin.” The consequences of sin remained, but the relationship was restored. Psalm 51 records his prayer from that time.

The way to adjust is to stop saying “He is the man” and start saying “I am the man.” Not self-punishment, but honesty. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to gently point out one thing, as Nathan did, and then respond as David did: “I have sinned.”
lessons.light: Pride is leaving our proper place; humility is returning to it. Adam said, “It was her.” David said, “It was me.” The first deepens the rift; the second opens a way for grace to come in. Humility is the key to revival: God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. Confession isn’t failure; it is the beginning of coming back into the light.
think: In 2 Samuel 12:5-7, how did David’s judgment of others differ from his judgment of himself?
Whom have I criticized lately when, in fact, “I am the man”?
To God, or to which person, do I need to say, “I was wrong”?
lessons.speak: Father, like David I often see others’ sins clearly and my own only dimly. Holy Spirit, shine your light on me gently, as Nathan did. I won’t shift the blame anymore; I am willing to say, “I have sinned.” Thank you for your forgiveness, and help me repair the relationships that have been hurt because of me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Spend five quiet minutes today asking the Holy Spirit to show you one thing you often blame others for but share responsibility for yourself. If you have hurt someone, offer a brief apology today or this week—with no “but” attached.
lessons.quick: Adam said, “It was her.” David said, “It was me.”
text: The LORD sent Nathan to David. He came to him, and said to him, “There were two men in one city: the one rich, and the other poor.
The rich man had very many flocks and herds,

but the poor man had nothing, except one little ewe lamb, which he had bought and raised. It grew up together with him and with his children. It ate of his own food, drank of his own cup, and lay in his bosom, and was like a daughter to him.

A traveler came to the rich man, and he didn’t want to take of his own flock and of his own herd to prepare for the wayfaring man who had come to him, but took the poor man’s lamb and prepared it for the man who had come to him.”
David’s anger burned hot against the man, and he said to Nathan, “As the LORD lives, the man who has done this deserves to die!
He must restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing and because he had no pity!”
Nathan said to David, “You are the man! This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you out of the hand of Saul.

I gave you your master’s house and your master’s wives into your bosom, and gave you the house of Israel and of Judah; and if that would have been too little, I would have added to you many more such things.

Why have you despised the LORD’s word, to do that which is evil in his sight? You have struck Uriah the Hittite with the sword, have taken his wife to be your wife, and have slain him with the sword of the children of Ammon.
Now therefore the sword will never depart from your house, because you have despised me and have taken Uriah the Hittite’s wife to be your wife.’

“This is what the LORD says: ‘Behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house; and I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he will lie with your wives in the sight of this sun.
For you did this secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel, and before the sun.’”
David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against the LORD.” Nathan said to David, “The LORD also has put away your sin. You will not die.

lessons.title: Fellowship in the Light
lessons.hear:
This week we stepped into the scene of humanity’s relational accident. Adam hid and shifted the blame. James showed that our fights come from the desires within us. Cain killed his brother out of envy. David covered up his sin until Nathan exposed it. These stories may feel heavy, but in every one of them there is a God who doesn’t give up: he calls, he warns, he sends prophets, he forgives.

John sums all of this up in a picture of light: “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5). Sin drives people into the dark, and wherever we hide, relationships wither. But John goes on: “But if we walk in the light as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7). Notice the order here: when we step into the light, the result isn’t only fellowship with God, but “fellowship with one another.” Honesty is sunlight for a relationship; covering up is its shadow.

Then comes a beautiful promise: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins” (1 John 1:9). The cross means we never have to hide again, because sin now has a way out.

Repetition means asking yourself every night: Did I hide, blame, or envy today? Then bring it to God in the light. The app’s Word Watch can help you review your day each evening with three questions. Multiplication means finding a trustworthy spiritual companion and agreeing together to walk in the light—sharing your weaknesses and praying for each other. Friendships like that don’t have to be perfect, only real, because wherever there is honesty, there is light.
lessons.light: The “2” in 235 means becoming spiritual companions with selfless people. Such companions don’t perform for each other; they have fellowship in the light. The self-centered person is afraid of being seen. The selfless person isn’t, because their worth has already been settled by the blood of Christ. Change begins with me: I step into the light first.
think: According to 1 John 1:7, what two results come from walking in the light?
Which story this week shone the most light into the darkness of my heart?
Whom will I invite to agree with me to have fellowship in the light?
lessons.speak: Father, you are light, and in you is no darkness at all. Thank you that the blood of your Son Jesus cleanses me from all sin, so I never have to hide again. Help me walk in the light every day, and give me a spiritual companion so that we can be honest with each other, pray for each other, and walk in the light together. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, meet with a trustworthy brother or sister of the same sex. Each share one relational weakness from this week, then pray for each other, and agree to share again in a month.
lessons.quick: Honesty is sunlight for a relationship; covering up is its shadow.
text: This is the message which we have heard from him and announce to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
If we say that we have fellowship with him and walk in the darkness, we lie and don’t tell the truth.
But if we walk in the light as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin.
If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

weeks.title: The Cross: Center of Reconciliation
weeks.theme: The vertical beam of the cross reconciles us to God; the horizontal beam reconciles us to one another.
group: Read 2 Corinthians 5:17-18. Who gives “the ministry of reconciliation,” and to whom?
Is there a “middle wall of separation” in your life, and how did it get built?
Which relationship are you willing to take one small step toward reconciling this week, and what exactly will you do?
weeks.sunday: Choose a relationship that has cooled a bit—a relative, a former coworker, or someone at church. Write a short card or send a message to greet and bless them, without bringing up the past. Before you write, pray at the foot of the cross and ask the Lord to remove any bitterness from you. Once it’s sent, however they respond, leave the outcome with God, and thank him for reconciling with you first.

lessons.title: The Ministry of Reconciliation
lessons.hear:
Last week we saw how sin tears relationships apart: people are cut off from God, and they blame, envy, and hurt one another. So how can broken relationships be mended? Paul gives the answer: “But all things are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18).

Notice that reconciliation is “of God.” It doesn’t begin with us turning back first, apologizing first, or proving we’re good enough. God makes the first move. Paul says, “For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). On the cross, Jesus paid the price for every rift. That’s why we often say the cross has two beams: the vertical beam joins heaven and earth, reconciling us to God; the horizontal beam stretches out left and right, reconciling us to one another.

This reconciliation brings a brand-new identity: “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17). It also brings a brand-new way of seeing people: “Therefore we know no one according to the flesh from now on” (2 Corinthians 5:16). I no longer define a person by their education, income, opinions, or past mistakes. I see them through the lens of the cross: this, too, is someone Christ died for.

Finally, God has handed “the ministry of reconciliation” to us. It isn’t reserved for pastors; it is the calling of everyone God has reconciled. Like someone pulled ashore who turns around and becomes a lifeguard, we who have been reconciled are sent out to build bridges. In our extended families, workplaces, neighborhoods, and online spaces, we are Christ’s ambassadors, carrying the message of reconciliation.
lessons.light: Two core commitments: let Jesus reign, and let Jesus receive all the glory. Reconciliation doesn’t depend on our social skills; “all things are of God.” Moving from a human point of view to God’s point of view: we no longer know anyone according to the flesh but see every person through the lens of the cross. This is the foundation for building God’s system.
think: In 2 Corinthians 5:16-18, what new identity and new way of seeing does reconciliation bring?
By what standard do I most often know people “according to the flesh”?
How can I see one person through the lens of the cross today?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that while I was still your enemy, you reconciled me to yourself through Christ. You made him who knew no sin to be sin for me, and you made me a new creation. Help me no longer know anyone according to the flesh, and make me faithful in the ministry of reconciliation you have entrusted to me, building bridges between people. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose someone you tend to see through a “label”—a difficult coworker or relative, for example. Pray for them, and look for a chance to give them a sincere word of affirmation.
lessons.quick: All things are of God: he reconciled first, so we can urge others to be reconciled.
text: For the love of Christ compels us; because we judge thus: that one died for all, therefore all died.
He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.
Therefore we know no one according to the flesh from now on. Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no more.
Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.
But all things are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation;
namely, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning to them their trespasses, and having committed to us the word of reconciliation.
We are therefore ambassadors on behalf of Christ, as though God were entreating by us: we beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.
For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

lessons.title: Breaking Down the Middle Wall
lessons.hear:
A Chinese church had two groups of people. One was the second generation, raised locally and most comfortable in English. The other was newly arrived immigrants from many places who spoke only Mandarin. The two groups sat in the same sanctuary, yet it was as if an invisible wall stood between them. The new immigrants felt looked down on; the second generation felt they couldn’t understand or find a way in. Eventually they even sat on opposite sides at lunch.

This isn’t a new problem. In Paul’s day there was a real wall between Jews and Gentiles: a barrier in the temple courts that Gentiles could not pass. Religion, culture, food, and history divided them at every turn. Yet Paul declares: “For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation” (Ephesians 2:14).

Our old mindset often says: people are just different; if we get along, we spend time together, and if we don’t, we keep our distance. But God’s view is that the cross didn’t only break down the wall between people and God; it broke down the walls between people too. Jesus came to “reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, having killed the hostility through it” (Ephesians 2:16). He didn’t turn Jews into Gentiles or Gentiles into Jews. Instead, “he might create in himself one new man of the two, making peace” (Ephesians 2:15). Unity doesn’t erase differences; it gives us a larger shared identity in Christ.

That church later started “bilingual tables.” Each table was deliberately mixed, someone helped translate, and people took turns sharing dishes from their hometowns and stories of how they came to faith. The wall didn’t come down in a day, but every meal knocked out another brick. They discovered that people who had been strangers were family at the foot of the cross.
lessons.light: Self-centered socializing only connects with “people like me.” Selfless love is willing to cross the wall. Relationships matter more than things—and more than our opinions and habits. Letting Jesus reign means letting his cross be bigger than my preferences. Unity doesn’t mean everyone becomes the same; it means being in Christ together, like different instruments in an orchestra making harmony under one conductor.
think: In Ephesians 2:14-16, how did Jesus break down the dividing wall?
What wall stands near me: generation, language, politics, or social class?
Which brick can I knock out, and with whom can I share a meal?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, on the cross you broke down the middle wall of separation and made those far off and those near into one body. I confess that I often spend time only with people like me and keep my distance from those who are different. Enlarge my heart so that I am willing to cross the wall and become family with others in you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week at church or at work, deliberately sit next to someone whose background differs from yours—in age, language, or ethnicity. Ask them a question about their hometown or their life, and listen attentively.
lessons.quick: The cross breaks down not only the wall between us and God but also the walls between us and others.
text: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off are made near in the blood of Christ.
For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation,
having abolished in his flesh the hostility, the law of commandments contained in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man of the two, making peace,
and might reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, having killed the hostility through it.
He came and preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near.
For through him we both have our access in one Spirit to the Father.

lessons.title: Peace Through the Cross
lessons.hear:
In Colossians, Paul says that Christ came “having made peace through the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20). Peace doesn’t come from the negotiating table but from a cross—not from someone winning, but from a Lord who willingly lost everything. Then he reminds the Colossian believers: “You, being in past times alienated and enemies in your mind in your evil deeds” (Colossians 1:21). We were once God’s enemies, but he didn’t wait for us to back down first. He came toward us first.

Those who have been reconciled learn to reconcile. Today’s practice is to take one small step toward a relationship that is broken or has gone cold. Notice: one small step, not the whole journey at once. Maybe you pray for that person for a week first. Maybe you send a short greeting. Maybe you take the initiative to say hello at a family gathering. Maybe you write down the part you yourself need to apologize for.

As you take that step, remember a few things. First, reconciliation takes two people; you can only be responsible for your side. Paul says, “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men” (Romans 12:18). “If it is possible” admits that sometimes the other person isn’t ready yet. Second, forgiveness doesn’t mean denying the hurt, nor does it mean instantly restoring trust. Third, if the relationship involves violence, harassment, threats, or fraud, safety comes first. You can leave judgment with God in your heart while keeping your distance and seeking help from trusted people or professionals.

Reconciliation at the cross is sometimes a hug, sometimes a greeting, and sometimes simply a prayer that stops cursing and starts blessing. Whatever form it takes, it lets the peace of Christ rule in your life.
lessons.light: Self-denial is for Jesus and for others, not for ourselves. Taking a step toward reconciliation often means laying down the self-centered “Why should I go first?” But selflessness doesn’t mean having no boundaries. Letting God be God means handing the other person’s response over to him. Change starts with me, but the outcome isn’t mine to control; I am responsible to obey, and God is responsible to bring it to completion.
think: In Colossians 1:20-22, how did God treat us when we were his enemies?
Is there someone about whom my heart says, “Why should I go first?”
What is the smallest step I could take toward this relationship today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you made peace through the blood of your cross, and you came toward me while I was still your enemy. Give me courage to take one small step toward a broken relationship, and give me wisdom to know when to draw near and when to wait. I place the outcome in your hands. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Take the smallest step today toward a relationship that has gone cold or broken: pray specifically for the other person for three minutes, or send a short greeting with no accusation in it. If there are any safety concerns, talk with someone you trust first.
lessons.quick: Reconciliation starts with one small step, and the outcome rests in God’s hands.
text: For all the fullness was pleased to dwell in him,
and through him to reconcile all things to himself by him, whether things on the earth or things in the heavens, having made peace through the blood of his cross.
You, being in past times alienated and enemies in your mind in your evil deeds,
yet now he has reconciled in the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and without defect and blameless before him,

lessons.title: It Was God Who Sent Me
lessons.hear:
Out of envy, Joseph’s brothers sold him into Egypt. More than twenty years later, they came to buy grain and found themselves bowing before Joseph—now the second most powerful man in Egypt—without recognizing him. Joseph held enormous power. He could have taken revenge, or simply never revealed who he was. But he didn’t reveal himself right away. First he tested them to see whether they had changed (see Genesis 42:9-17). Only when Judah offered to take the punishment in place of their youngest brother, Benjamin, was Joseph sure they were no longer the men they once had been.

Then Joseph “wept aloud” and said to them: “I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold into Egypt. Now don’t be grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that you sold me here” (Genesis 45:4-5). He didn’t pretend the harm never happened; he said plainly, “whom you sold.” But he also saw a greater hand at work: “So now it wasn’t you who sent me here, but God” (Genesis 45:8).

This story lets us review ourselves from two angles. If I am one of the brothers: have I ever hurt someone out of envy or selfishness and pretended for years that nothing happened? Judah’s change shows us that true repentance is a willingness to pay a price in order to love. If I am Joseph: am I keeping the person who hurt me locked in the past forever? Joseph’s forgiveness wasn’t naive. He took time to confirm that they had changed—that was wisdom. But in the end he chose not to take revenge—that was grace.

The key to adjusting is perspective. Joseph could forgive because he saw what had happened to him from God’s point of view. When we see only “what he did to me,” our hearts stay bound. When we see “what God has done through all of this,” our hearts are set free.
lessons.light: Move from an earthly point of view to a heavenly one, from the temporary to the eternal. Joseph didn’t deny the harm, but he left judgment with God, and so he became the salvation of his family. The focus isn’t on others or on circumstances but on Jesus. Forgiveness doesn’t mean instantly restoring trust; wisdom and grace can walk together, just as they did for Joseph.
think: In Genesis 45:4-8, how did Joseph face both the harm done to him and God’s purpose?
In this story, am I more like the brothers or like Joseph?
How do I need to adjust the way I see an old wound?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that you were still in control in Joseph’s suffering, and that you are still at work in my wounds. If I have hurt others as Joseph’s brothers did, give me a heart of true repentance. If I have been hurt as Joseph was, help me see it from your point of view and leave judgment with you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down an old hurt you still haven’t let go of, and beside it write one sentence: “What God may have done through this.” If you have hurt someone, consider this week how you might acknowledge it to them.
lessons.quick: Joseph didn’t deny the harm, but he saw a greater hand at work.
text: Then Joseph couldn’t control himself before all those who stood before him, and he called out, “Cause everyone to go out from me!” No one else stood with him, while Joseph made himself known to his brothers.
He wept aloud. The Egyptians heard, and the house of Pharaoh heard.
Joseph said to his brothers, “I am Joseph! Does my father still live?” His brothers couldn’t answer him; for they were terrified at his presence.
Joseph said to his brothers, “Come near to me, please.” They came near. He said, “I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold into Egypt.
Now don’t be grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life.
For these two years the famine has been in the land, and there are yet five years, in which there will be no plowing and no harvest.
God sent me before you to preserve for you a remnant on the earth, and to save you alive by a great deliverance.
So now it wasn’t you who sent me here, but God, and he has made me a father to Pharaoh, lord of all his house, and ruler over all the land of Egypt.

lessons.title: Built Together into God’s Household
lessons.hear:
This week we stood before the cross. We saw that God reconciled us to himself first and then entrusted the ministry of reconciliation to us. We saw that the cross broke down the middle wall of separation. We practiced taking a small step toward a broken relationship, and in Joseph’s story we saw how forgiveness and wisdom go hand in hand. Now let’s put all of this into a larger picture: God is building a household.

Paul says, “So then you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19). Reconciliation doesn’t only mean two people stop fighting. It means a group of people who once had nothing to do with each other—who were even enemies—are being built into a house, “Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone; in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord” (Ephesians 2:20-21).

Notice the word “grows.” Building God’s household is a process. Just as a house goes up brick by brick, reconciliation accumulates one act at a time. Every time you choose not to forward gossip in a group chat, every time you say “I’m sorry” first to your family, every time you welcome a new friend who is different from you, you lay another brick in God’s house.

Repetition means pausing before the cross each day to ask: Am I tearing down walls today, or building them? The app’s Reconciliation Guide can walk with you step by step as you think through a relationship. Multiplication means passing on the message of reconciliation. You could share with your small group the small step you took this week, or pray with a friend who is hurting in a relationship. We are not only reconciled people; we are ambassadors of reconciliation.
lessons.light: One purpose: build God’s system. God’s household isn’t built by perfect people but by reconciled people who are “built together.” The order of the five-fold change is life first, then relationships, then ministry.
