A life changed by the cross naturally overflows into reconciled relationships, which then grow into ministry that builds God’s household.
think: In Ephesians 2:19-22, what does God build reconciled people into?
Where did I “tear down walls” this week, and where did I “build” them?
With whom will I share this week’s experience of reconciliation, or walk alongside for a step?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that I am no longer a stranger and foreigner but a member of your household. Use me as a brick in your house, tearing down walls and building bridges in my family, my church, and my community. And let me pass the message of reconciliation on to someone who needs it. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, share with your small group the small step you took toward a relationship (without naming the other person), and invite a group member to pray with you for each other’s journeys toward reconciliation.
lessons.quick: Reconciled people grow together into God’s household.
text: So then you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and of the household of God,
being built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone;
in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord;
in whom you also are built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit.

weeks.keyText: But all things are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation;

weeks.title: Living for Others’ Approval
weeks.theme: People-pleasing, saving face, and fear of rejection all grow from loving people’s praise more than God’s.
group: Read John 12:42-43. Why didn’t those rulers dare to confess Jesus?
Whose opinion do you care about most, and has that ever led you to do something against your conscience?
How will you do something good for someone “in secret” this week? What’s your plan?
weeks.sunday: Do something good in secret for a neighbor, a cleaner, or someone who serves at church—for example, leave an unsigned thank-you card and a small snack. Before you do it, pray: “Father, this is for your eyes only.” Afterward, don’t take photos and don’t share it. Just tell God, “Thank you for seeing in secret. Your delight is enough for me.”

lessons.title: Loving People’s Praise More Than God’s
lessons.hear:
John’s Gospel records a heartbreaking scene. Jesus had done many miracles, and “even many of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they didn’t confess it, so that they wouldn’t be put out of the synagogue” (John 12:42). In their hearts they believed, but they didn’t dare say so. Why? John goes straight to the point: “for they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise” (John 12:43).

The word for “praise” here is the same word often translated “glory,” and in the Hebrew of the Old Testament, glory carries the sense of “weight”—being taken seriously. Everyone carries a set of scales in their heart that measures what matters. For these rulers, the opinion of their peers, their position in the synagogue, and acceptance by their group weighed more than God’s pleasure. Once those scales are tipped, a whole life tips with them: we speak after checking people’s faces, act after gauging their reactions, and even measure our faith by what others think.

Jesus lived in a completely different way. He said, “I don’t receive glory from men” (John 5:41). It isn’t that he didn’t care about people; he just didn’t live on their applause. Then he asked a searching question: “How can you believe, who receive glory from one another, and you don’t seek the glory that comes from the only God?” (John 5:44). When we are busy liking and lifting up one another, there’s no room left to look up to God.

This is the great sickness of our age. Likes on social media, replies in group chats, comparisons at class reunions—they all keep asking us, “Are you good enough? What do people think of you?” But the gospel gives a brand-new answer: in Christ, you are already valued and loved by God the Father. A child who knows their parents love them deeply doesn’t need to perform for every stranger. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to set the scales in your heart straight.
lessons.light: Self-centered socializing revolves around “me” and cares about “What do others think of me?” The selfless life revolves around God and cares about “What does God think?” When I let Jesus receive all the glory, I no longer need to grab glory from people. The focus is on Jesus—not on myself, and not on others. This is the shift from a worldly point of view to God’s point of view.
think: In John 5:44, what does Jesus say is the result of receiving glory from one another?
On the scales of my heart, whose opinion weighs the most?
In which situation today can I choose to seek only God’s pleasure?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that I often love people’s praise more than yours. I care too much about how others see me and respond to me, so much that I don’t dare speak the truth or stand up for you. Set the scales in my heart straight, and let me know that in Christ I am already valued by you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, notice three times when you say something or make a decision “because of what others will think,” and write them down. Tonight, bring them to God and ask him to show you the fear behind them.
lessons.quick: When the scales of the heart are set straight, life stops tilting.
text: I don’t receive glory from men.
But I know you, that you don’t have God’s love in yourselves.
I have come in my Father’s name, and you don’t receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him.
How can you believe, who receive glory from one another, and you don’t seek the glory that comes from the only God?

lessons.title: Please Honor Me Before the People
lessons.hear:
A sister who was the eldest child in her family had always been “the sensible one.” Weddings and funerals for relatives, every request from her younger siblings—she never said no. When coworkers asked her to cover their shifts, she always said yes. On the surface she was well liked, but inside she grew more and more exhausted, often crying alone late at night. One day in prayer she realized: “I don’t say yes because I love them. I say yes because I’m afraid they won’t like me.”

We often carry an old mindset: pleasing people is loving them, and never saying no is what a good Christian does. But Saul’s story shows us another side. God commanded him to completely destroy the Amalekites, but he kept the best of the cattle and sheep. When Samuel rebuked him, he told the truth: “I have sinned; for I have transgressed the commandment of the LORD and your words, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice” (1 Samuel 15:24). Saul’s problem wasn’t that he didn’t love the people; it was that he was too afraid of them.

Even sadder is what he said next: “I have sinned; yet please honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel” (1 Samuel 15:30). Even while confessing, what he cared about most was saving face. This is the deepest bondage of a people-pleasing personality: even repentance has to protect the image.

God’s view is this: “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22). Love isn’t endless people-pleasing; it is obeying God and truly seeking the other person’s good. Sometimes love means saying “no.” That sister began learning to pray before agreeing to things, and she learned to decline gently. “I turned down a few things,” she said, “but for the first time, when I said ‘yes,’ I really meant it.”
lessons.light: People-pleasing looks selfless, but it is actually self-centered: it is driven by fear of losing others’ approval. True selflessness hands our reputation over to God and obeys his will. Letting Jesus reign means letting him decide whether I say “yes” or “no.” Boundaries aren’t a lack of love; they bring love back to what is real. Only those who stand firm before God can be free before people.
think: In 1 Samuel 15:24 and 15:30, what did Saul care about most?
Which recent “yes” of mine actually came from fear of being disliked?
Is there something I need to gently say “no” to after praying?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that like Saul I often fear the people—saying yes so I’ll be liked and compromising to save face. Set me free from the bondage of people-pleasing and establish me in your love. Teach me to say a sincere “yes” and a gentle “no,” always seeking your pleasure. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, when someone asks you for help, first say, “Let me think about it and get back to you.” Pray for one minute, then decide whether to agree wholeheartedly or to decline gently.
lessons.quick: Love isn’t endless people-pleasing; sometimes love means saying “no.”
text: Samuel said, “Has the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the LORD’s voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.
For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as idolatry and teraphim. Because you have rejected the LORD’s word, he has also rejected you from being king.”
Saul said to Samuel, “I have sinned; for I have transgressed the commandment of the LORD and your words, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice.
Now therefore, please pardon my sin, and turn again with me, that I may worship the LORD.”
Samuel said to Saul, “I will not return with you; for you have rejected the LORD’s word, and the LORD has rejected you from being king over Israel.”
As Samuel turned around to go away, Saul grabbed the skirt of his robe, and it tore.
Samuel said to him, “The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today, and has given it to a neighbor of yours who is better than you.
Also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent; for he is not a man, that he should repent.”
Then he said, “I have sinned; yet please honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel, and come back with me, that I may worship the LORD your God.”

lessons.title: Doing Good in Secret
lessons.hear:
In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus teaches a very practical exercise for healing a heart that lives for others’ approval: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them” (Matthew 6:1). He gives three examples: giving, prayer, and fasting. All three are good things, but if they are done to be seen, “they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:2). People’s applause is all the payment they will get.

Jesus offers a striking image: “don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matthew 6:3). In other words, don’t even keep close track yourself of how much good you have done, let alone show it off or keep score. Then comes a warm promise: “your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly” (Matthew 6:4).

This doesn’t mean every good deed must be hidden. Jesus also said to let people see our good works so that they glorify our Father in heaven. The key is motive: am I doing this so people will see me, or so they will see God? Doing good in secret is like weight training for the soul; it specifically strengthens the part of us that doesn’t need an audience.

Try it today. Quietly restock the copy paper at the office. In your neighborhood group chat, anonymously help an older person sort out something they couldn’t figure out how to do. Buy breakfast for an often-overlooked classmate and leave it on their desk. Or, in prayer, spend ten minutes interceding for someone without ever telling them. No photos, no check-ins, no hints—let only your heavenly Father know. You’ll discover that love meant for God’s eyes alone carries a special kind of freedom.
lessons.light: Self-denial is for Jesus and for others, not for ourselves. Doing good in secret is a great way to practice selflessness: laying down the need to be seen and seeking only the Father’s pleasure. When I let Jesus receive all the glory, my good deeds are no longer medals for me but gifts for God. Relying on the Holy Spirit with your heart rather than being driven by applause, love can go the distance.
think: In Matthew 6:1-4, how does Jesus describe two different kinds of reward?
When I do good, how much of it is about being seen?
For whom will I do something good in secret today?
lessons.speak: Father, you see in secret. I confess that I often want my good deeds to be seen and praised. Today I want to do something good in secret for someone, seeking no return and no applause—only your pleasure. May this love be a gift to you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, do something good in secret for a coworker, classmate, or neighbor—prepare breakfast for them, say, or take care of a small chore. Don’t sign it, don’t take a photo, and don’t tell anyone.
lessons.quick: Love meant for God’s eyes alone carries a special kind of freedom.
text: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.

Therefore, when you do merciful deeds, don’t sound a trumpet before yourself, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may get glory from men. Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward.
But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does,
so that your merciful deeds may be in secret, then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.

“When you pray, you shall not be as the hypocrites, for they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen by men. Most certainly, I tell you, they have received their reward.
But you, when you pray, enter into your inner room, and having shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.

lessons.title: Peter Drew Back
lessons.hear:
Peter was one of the first apostles to understand that the gospel makes no distinction between Jews and Gentiles. He had seen the Holy Spirit fall on Gentiles in Cornelius’s house, and he had defended this in Jerusalem. But in Antioch something sad happened. He had been eating with Gentile believers, “But when they came, he drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision” (Galatians 2:12).

A great apostle quietly changed tables because he was afraid of what a certain group would think. Worse still, his retreat pulled others along: “And the rest of the Jews joined him in his hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was carried away with their hypocrisy” (Galatians 2:13). The fear of people is contagious. And what would those Gentile believers who were left out have thought? “So we’re not good enough.”

Let this mirror show you yourself. At a class reunion, am I afraid of being laughed at, so I don’t admit I’m a Christian? At a company dinner, do I watch my boss’s face and freeze out an unpopular coworker? At church, do I sit only with the “important people”? The fear of people usually doesn’t look like doing something terrible. It looks like quietly “changing tables.”

The good news is that Peter didn’t stay there. After Paul confronted him face to face, Peter later declared clearly at the Jerusalem council: “But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are” (Acts 15:11). Years later, in his letter, he called Paul “our beloved brother Paul” (2 Peter 3:15). Corrected, repentant, restored—Peter didn’t cut Paul off to save face; he became a more genuine man. The way to adjust is to turn from fearing people back to fearing God, and then go back to that table.
lessons.light: Pride sometimes looks like timidity: we fear losing status and acceptance, yet we are still centered on ourselves. “The fear of man proves to be a snare, but whoever puts his trust in the LORD is kept safe” (Proverbs 29:25). Peter’s restoration reminds us that being corrected isn’t humiliation; it is a chance to return to our proper place.
think: In Galatians 2:12-13, what consequences did Peter’s fear bring?
In what situation have I quietly “changed tables” because I was afraid of people?
How will I go back to that table and welcome the person I left out?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that like Peter I have drawn back and played the hypocrite because I feared what people would think, and I have left out those I should have welcomed. Thank you for restoring Peter, and for restoring me. Help me fear you more than I fear people, and to accept correction humbly. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of someone you have left out because of what others might think. Take the initiative to greet them, sit beside them, or send them a friendly message.
lessons.quick: The fear of people often looks like quietly changing tables.
text: But when Peter came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he stood condemned.
For before some people came from James, he ate with the Gentiles. But when they came, he drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision.
And the rest of the Jews joined him in his hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was carried away with their hypocrisy.

But when I saw that they didn’t walk uprightly according to the truth of the Good News, I said to Peter before them all, “If you, being a Jew, live as the Gentiles do, and not as the Jews do, why do you compel the Gentiles to live as the Jews do?

lessons.title: Pleasing the God Who Tests Our Hearts
lessons.hear:
This week we faced a deep bondage: living for other people’s approval. We saw rulers who loved people’s praise more than God’s. We saw Saul trying to save face even as he confessed. We practiced doing good in secret, and we saw ourselves in Peter changing tables. Now let’s look at how someone who has been set free from this bondage loves people.

Paul says, “so we speak—not as pleasing men, but God, who tests our hearts” (1 Thessalonians 2:4). You might assume someone who doesn’t try to please people must be cold. But look at what comes next: “But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children” (1 Thessalonians 2:7). And again: “we were well pleased to impart to you not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls” (1 Thessalonians 2:8).

Here’s the secret: only someone who doesn’t need glory from people can truly give. A people-pleaser is actually “taking” in relationships—taking affirmation, taking acceptance. Only those satisfied by God’s love can give unconditionally, like a mother. Not pleasing people doesn’t mean not loving them; it means we are finally free to love them.

Repetition means saying to God each morning, “Today I only want to please you.” Multiplication means passing this freedom on. There may be a friend near you who is worn out from living for others’ approval—maybe a young person who is always waiting for replies in the group chat. Take them out for coffee and tell them, “In God’s eyes, you are already valued.” Your words might be the beginning of the scales in their heart being set straight.
lessons.light: The “3” in 235 is the relationship of spiritual parents and children. Paul nurturing believers like a mother is exactly what that relationship looks like. Selflessness isn’t having nothing; it is entering the limitless: no longer taking from people, but giving endlessly out of what we receive from God. When Jesus receives all the glory, I am set free.
think: In 1 Thessalonians 2:4-8, Paul didn’t aim to please people—so how did he treat them?
In what area have I begun to experience freedom from people’s opinions this week?
Which friend who lives for others’ approval will I walk alongside?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for testing my heart and loving me deeply. I no longer need glory from people, because your pleasure is enough. Make me like Paul, loving people gently and giving away both the gospel and my own life. And let me bring this freedom to a friend. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, meet for coffee or call a friend who worries a lot about what others think. Listen to how they’re doing, and before you finish, tell them: “In God’s eyes, you are already valued.”
lessons.quick: Not pleasing people doesn’t mean not loving them; it means we are finally free to love.
text: But even as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the Good News, so we speak—not as pleasing men, but God, who tests our hearts.
For neither were we at any time found using words of flattery, as you know, nor a cloak of covetousness (God is witness),
nor seeking glory from men (neither from you nor from others), when we might have claimed authority as apostles of Christ.
But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children.
Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.

weeks.keyText: for they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise.

weeks.title: Pride: Leaving Our Place Among People
weeks.theme: Pride makes us compete, judge, and insist on winning; humility returns us to our proper place—letting people be people and God be God.
group: Read Luke 18:9-14. Where was the focus of the Pharisee’s prayer, and where was the focus of the tax collector’s?
In what situations are you most tempted to “win”—arguments, comparisons, or being affirmed?
With whom are you willing to “take the lowest place” or serve first this week? What is one concrete step?
weeks.sunday: At a meal or gathering, deliberately be the last to get your food, take the initiative to sit beside someone you don’t know well or who is quieter, and stay afterward to help clean up. Before you go, pray: “Lord, you are among us as one who serves—make me like you.” When you get home, thank God for one person you met today and pray for them.

lessons.title: Two Men Went Up to Pray
lessons.hear:
Proverbs names the most common root of conflict between people in a single line: “Pride only breeds quarrels, but wisdom is with people who take advice” (Proverbs 13:10). Pride isn’t always loud. It often dresses respectably—it can even show up in our prayers.

Jesus told a parable “to certain people who were convinced of their own righteousness, and who despised all others” (Luke 18:9). Two men went up to the temple to pray: a Pharisee and a tax collector. The Pharisee “stood and prayed by himself,” and his prayer was all about himself: I’m not a swindler or unjust like other people; I fast, I give. And he added one more line: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men … or even like this tax collector” (Luke 18:11). On the surface his prayer was addressed to God, but it was really a comparison, with himself as the star and the man he looked down on as the supporting cast.

The tax collector, however, was “standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his chest, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’” (Luke 18:13). He didn’t compare himself to anyone or defend himself. He simply stood in his proper place as a sinner and looked to God’s mercy. Jesus said it was this man who went home justified.

This parable shows us what pride looks like in relationships: it needs someone “worse than me” to make itself look good. At class reunions, in company meetings, in church small groups, pride quietly asks, “Who’s better than me? Who’s not as good as me?” Humility isn’t putting yourself down. It is stopping the comparison and returning to our proper place before God: a sinner in need of grace. Someone standing there no longer needs to beat anyone.
lessons.light: Pride means leaving our proper place and grasping power—leaving our place as human beings and trying to sit in the seat of judgment over others. Humility means laying down power and returning to our proper place: letting people be people and God be God. The Pharisee lost God in his comparisons; the tax collector found God in his confession. God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.
think: In Luke 18:11-13, how did the focus of the two men’s prayers differ?
With whom have I been comparing myself lately, saying in my heart, “I’m not like him”?
How can I pray from the tax collector’s place today?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that I am often like that Pharisee, using others to make myself look good in my heart—comparing even while I pray. Be merciful to me, a sinner. Bring me back to my proper place before you, where I no longer need to beat anyone and rely only on your grace. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, whenever the thought “I’m not like him” crosses your mind, stop immediately, pray a one-line blessing for that person, and tell God, “Lord, I need your mercy too.”
lessons.quick: Pride needs someone worse than me; humility needs only God’s mercy.
text: He also spoke this parable to certain people who were convinced of their own righteousness, and who despised all others:
“Two men went up into the temple to pray; one was a Pharisee, and the other was a tax collector.
The Pharisee stood and prayed by himself like this: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men: extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.
I fast twice a week. I give tithes of all that I get.’
But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his chest, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.”

lessons.title: Don’t Take the Best Seat
lessons.hear:
A brother who had worked hard for years was promoted to manager. He noticed he had changed. At class reunions he found himself casually mentioning his salary and title. At family dinners, if someone else’s child scored higher on exams than his, he went quiet. At church, if the ministry team didn’t adopt his suggestion, he didn’t feel like going for weeks. One day his wife asked him, “Why do you have to win at everything?” He was stunned and had no answer.

At a dinner party, Jesus noticed something: “how they chose the best seats” (Luke 14:7). In that culture, seating reflected status, and everyone wanted to sit near the front. Jesus didn’t say, “You should be a bit more humble.” He told a very practical parable. If you take the best seat yourself, the host may ask you to make room for someone more distinguished, and “Then you would begin, with shame, to take the lowest place” (Luke 14:9). But if you sit in the lowest place, the host may say, “Friend, move up higher” (Luke 14:10).

Our old mindset often says: you have to fight to get anything; if you don’t push yourself forward, people will look down on you. But Jesus says, “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). God’s view is that our place isn’t something we grab; it is something we are given. A seat you fought for is exhausting to keep—you’re always afraid someone will take it. A seat God gives you is a place of rest.

That brother began practicing one small thing: at any gathering, ask how others are doing first, and only talk about himself last. He was surprised to discover that when he stopped competing to talk, friends were more willing to open up to him. “It turns out,” he said, “that when I stop competing, relationships finally have room to grow.”
lessons.light: Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Grabbing the best seat is self-centered; taking the lowest place is selfless. Moving from a human point of view to God’s point of view: our place isn’t seized but given by God. Letting God be God means letting him decide where I sit. Only someone who has stopped grabbing for seats has room in their heart for others.
think: In Luke 14:8-11, what did Jesus observe, and what advice did he give?
Where do I most want the “best seat”—the floor in a conversation, saving face, or being affirmed?
At which gathering this week can I deliberately take “the lowest place”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you see that my heart is grabbing for the best seat too—I want to be seen, affirmed, and put up front. Forgive my competitiveness and make me content to sit in the lowest place, leaving my seating to you. Teach me to care for others first, so that relationships have room to grow. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: In any conversation or gathering today, first ask the other person two questions about how they’re doing, listen fully, and only then talk about yourself. Notice your urge to interrupt.
lessons.quick: A seat you fought for is exhausting to keep; a seat God gives is a place of rest.
text: He spoke a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the best seats, and said to them,
“When you are invited by anyone to a wedding feast, don’t sit in the best seat, since perhaps someone more honorable than you might be invited by him,
and he who invited both of you would come and tell you, ‘Make room for this person.’ Then you would begin, with shame, to take the lowest place.

But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when he who invited you comes, he may tell you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at the table with you.
For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

lessons.title: Among You as One Who Serves
lessons.hear:
On the night of the Last Supper, as Jesus was about to be betrayed, “A dispute also arose among them, which of them was considered to be greatest” (Luke 22:24). What an ironic picture: their Lord was about to lay down his life for them, and they were arguing about rankings. That’s how pride works—it pops up even in the holiest moments.

Jesus didn’t rebuke them loudly. Instead he redefined “great.” The kings of the Gentiles, he said, lord it over people and like to be called “benefactors.” “But not so with you. Rather, the one who is greater among you, let him become as the younger, and one who is governing, as one who serves” (Luke 22:26). Then he asked: who is greater, the one at the table or the one who serves? Common sense says the one at the table. But Jesus said, “But I am among you as one who serves” (Luke 22:27).

The kingdom’s ranking chart is upside down. The greatest isn’t the one served the most but the one who serves the most. This isn’t a cleverer social strategy; it is Jesus’ own life. He was Lord, yet he picked up a towel. He was King, yet he walked to the cross.

Today’s practice is to choose to be “as one who serves” in a specific social setting. In a meeting, affirm others’ ideas before offering your own. At a meal, refill everyone’s tea and look after the person sitting in the corner. In a heated group-chat argument, stop fighting for the last word and privately message the person who was embarrassed. If you are a manager, a group leader, or an elder, make a point today of bending down to ask a younger person, “How can I help you?” Serving doesn’t lower your status; it lives out your kingdom identity.
lessons.light: The “Serve” in the Way of Service means letting Jesus reign and serving others by his life. People matter more than tasks; don’t hurt people in a scramble for position. Selfless service isn’t a performance of humility; it is bending down before a real person. This is what building God’s system looks like day to day. Jesus is my example—he bent down first.
think: In Luke 22:25-27, how does Jesus redefine what it means to be “great”?
In which group am I more used to being served than serving?
In what setting today, and toward whom, will I be “as one who serves”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are Lord, yet you are among us as one who serves. I confess that I often want to be served and esteemed, and I rank people even in spiritual things. Give me a servant’s heart, so that today I bend down before a real person and live out what your kingdom looks like. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, in a group setting—a meeting, a meal, or a small group—take the initiative to do a task no one wants to do, and privately ask a younger or more marginal person, “How can I help you?”
lessons.quick: The kingdom’s ranking chart is upside down: the one who serves is greatest.
text: A dispute also arose among them, which of them was considered to be greatest.
He said to them, “The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called ‘benefactors.’
But not so with you. Rather, the one who is greater among you, let him become as the younger, and one who is governing, as one who serves.
For who is greater, one who sits at the table, or one who serves? Isn’t it he who sits at the table? But I am among you as one who serves.

lessons.title: He Is Able to Humble the Proud
lessons.hear:
Nebuchadnezzar was the most powerful man in the world in his day. One day, as he walked on the roof of his palace looking out over Babylon, his heart swelled with a sense of achievement: “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Daniel 4:30). Notice how much of that sentence is about “I” and “my.” This is pride in its classic form: taking credit for every achievement and forgetting who gave it.

Before the words had left his mouth, God’s judgment fell. He was driven away from people and ate grass like an animal, “until you know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men” (Daniel 4:32). God wasn’t humiliating him; God was healing him. A man who thought he was a god had to be brought down to the ground before he could lift his head and see heaven again.

Then came the turning point: “At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned to me; and I blessed the Most High” (Daniel 4:34). When he lifted his eyes to heaven, his sanity returned. Pride makes us lose our minds; humility restores us to our senses. In the end he said, “those who walk in pride he is able to abase” (Daniel 4:37).

Today, review yourself honestly. In your relationships, where is the “Didn’t I build this?” attitude? At home, do you feel “this family runs because of me”? In your fellowship, do you think “nothing would get done without me”? Among your friends, do you feel “they should all listen to me”? Pride makes us hard to approach. The first step of adjustment is to do what Nebuchadnezzar did and “lift up my eyes to heaven”: acknowledge that everything is God’s gift, and say thank you to the people I have run over.
lessons.light: Pride means leaving our proper place as human beings and grasping God’s power—trying to replace God. Nebuchadnezzar moving from “I have built” to “I blessed” is the move from self-centeredness back to our proper place. Humility overcomes pride. When we acknowledge that the Most High rules, we don’t need to be king in our relationships, and they can finally find rest. When I let Jesus reign, I can take off my crown.
think: Between Daniel 4:30 and 4:34, how did Nebuchadnezzar’s outlook change?
Where in my relationships do I carry an “it all depends on me” attitude?
Whom will I thank, acknowledging their contribution to my life?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that I often take credit for my achievements and think “it all depends on me”—at home, in my fellowship, and at work. Have mercy on me. Help me lift my eyes to heaven and acknowledge that everything is your gift. And let me see the people walking alongside me and thank them sincerely. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, tell someone you usually take for granted—your spouse, a parent, a co-worker, or someone who reports to you—specifically: “Thank you. I couldn’t have done this without you.”
lessons.quick: Pride makes us lose our minds; lifting our eyes to heaven restores us to our senses.
text: All this came on the King Nebuchadnezzar.
At the end of twelve months he was walking in the royal palace of Babylon.
The king spoke and said, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?”
While the word was in the king’s mouth, a voice came from the sky, saying, “O King Nebuchadnezzar, to you it is spoken: ‘The kingdom has departed from you.

You shall be driven from men, and your dwelling shall be with the animals of the field. You shall be made to eat grass like oxen. Seven times shall pass over you, until you know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he will.’”

This was fulfilled the same hour on Nebuchadnezzar. He was driven from men and ate grass like oxen; and his body was wet with the dew of the sky until his hair had grown like eagles’ feathers, and his nails like birds’ claws.

At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned to me; and I blessed the Most High, and I praised and honored him who lives forever, for his dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom from generation to generation.

All the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing; and he does according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth; and no one can stop his hand, or ask him, “What are you doing?”

At the same time my understanding returned to me; and for the glory of my kingdom, my majesty and brightness returned to me. My counselors and my lords sought me; and I was established in my kingdom, and excellent greatness was added to me.
Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven; for all his works are truth, and his ways justice; and those who walk in pride he is able to abase.

lessons.title: God Gives Grace to the Humble
lessons.hear:
This week we saw the many faces of pride among people: the Pharisee comparing himself in prayer, the guests grabbing the best seats, the disciples arguing over who was greatest, and the king saying, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built?” Every story tells us the same thing: “Pride only breeds quarrels” (Proverbs 13:10). But every story also points to a way home.

James says, “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’” (James 4:6). Notice what comes before that line: “he gives more grace.” Humility isn’t a virtue we squeeze out by willpower; it is our response to grace. Just as water always flows to the lowest place, God’s grace always flows to the humble.

James goes on to give a series of concrete actions: “Be subject therefore to God … Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you … Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you” (James 4:7-10). The order matters here: first we humble ourselves before God, and then we can be humble before people. Someone who often kneels before God doesn’t need to stand tall before others.

Repetition means spending a little time each day humbling yourself “in the sight of the Lord”: admitting your needs and thanking him for his grace. Multiplication means carrying humility into your relationships. Pride provokes pride, but humility inspires humility too. This week, at home or in your small group, you could be the first to say “I was wrong,” or the first to say “You have a point.” You could also share where you noticed your pride this week and invite a companion to practice humility with you.
lessons.light: Humility is the key to revival; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. “Repetition” in the eight steps means returning to our proper place every day; “multiplication” means letting humility spread through our relationships. When one person bows first, it becomes easier for the other to let go. Change starts with me—I don’t have to wait for the other person to change first. Selflessness defeats Satan’s attempts to divide.
think: What actions in response to God’s grace does James 4:7-10 list?
In which of this week’s stories did I see my own pride most clearly?
To whom will I be the first to say, “I was wrong” or “You have a point”?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that you give more grace. I want to humble myself before you, submit to you, and draw near to you. Let humility spread through my family, my church, and my friendships. Make me willing to be the first to bow and the first to admit I’m wrong, so that grace can flow among us. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, in a tense relationship, be the first to say “You have a point” or “I was wrong about this.” Also share your experience of practicing humility this week with a companion.
lessons.quick: Water flows to the lowest place, and grace always flows to the humble.
text: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners. Purify your hearts, you double-minded.
Lament, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom.
Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.

weeks.keyText: Pride only breeds quarrels, but wisdom is with people who take advice.

weeks.title: People Are Not Tools
weeks.theme: People bear God’s image; they are not contacts or resources, and selfless love seeks their good rather than our gain.
group: Read Philippians 2:3-4. How does Paul describe looking “to the things of others”?
Have you ever been “used” by someone—or have you ever treated someone as a tool?
What will you do this week for someone who “doesn’t have the resources to repay you”? Name a specific step.
weeks.sunday: Invite someone who can’t return the favor to share a meal—an older person living alone, a migrant worker, a student from a struggling family, or a friend who has just moved to a new city (feel free to bring family members or people from your small group along). Before you go, pray: “Lord, help me see that this person bears your image.” During the meal, listen to their story. When you get home, thank God for them and ask him to keep watching over them.

lessons.title: Looking to the Things of Others
lessons.hear:
We live in an age obsessed with “networking.” Business cards, messaging groups, and social-media connections are often seen as assets: What use is this person to me? What opportunities could knowing them bring? Without realizing it, people become tools and relationships become transactions.

In Philippians, Paul gives us an entirely different way of seeing: “each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others” (Philippians 2:4). Notice that Paul doesn’t say, “Don’t look to your own things.” He says, “not just.” Love doesn’t deny our own needs; it widens our gaze so that other people’s good also enters our hearts. The previous verse is even more specific: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself” (Philippians 2:3).

Where does love like this come from? Paul points straight to Jesus: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5). Christ, “existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6-7). If anyone in the universe had the right to “use” others, it was God. Yet he didn’t use us to serve himself; he gave himself up to make us whole.

This is the great divide in human relationships. The self-centered heart asks, “What use is this person to me?” The mind of Christ asks, “What use can I be to this person?” The first treats people as ladders; the second makes itself a bridge. Every person is made in God’s image. Their worth doesn’t lie in what they can do for me but in what God has done for them: Christ died for them. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to put the mind of Christ in your heart.
lessons.light: Self-denial: for Jesus and for others, not for ourselves. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Jesus is my example: he had every right, yet chose to empty himself. Turning from “Who is useful to me?” to “To whom can I be useful?” is the shift from the self-centered life to the selfless life. A ladder is thrown away once it has been used; a bridge carries people somewhere better.
think: In Philippians 2:3-7, how is looking “to the things of others” connected to Christ emptying himself?
In my relationships, do I unconsciously ask, “What use is this person to me?”
How can I look to the things of someone near me today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you existed in the form of God, yet you emptied yourself, took the form of a servant, and made me whole. I confess that I often treat people as tools, weighing how useful they are to me. Put your mind in my heart, so that I look not just to my own things but sincerely to the things of others. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, open your contacts or group chats and find someone you haven’t been in touch with for a long time and who “isn’t much use” to you. Send them a message to say hello and ask, “Is there anything I can pray for you about lately?”
lessons.quick: The self-centered heart asks, “What use is he to me?” The mind of Christ asks, “What can I do for him?”
text: If therefore there is any exhortation in Christ, if any consolation of love, if any fellowship of the Spirit, if any tender mercies and compassion,
make my joy full by being like-minded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind;
doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself;
each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.
Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus,
who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped,
but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.
And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.

lessons.title: Laban’s Ledger
lessons.hear:
A sister who had just joined a multilevel marketing business suddenly began warmly reaching out to college classmates she hadn’t seen in years and to people at church, inviting them for coffee or a meal. At first everyone was delighted—until the third meeting, when she pulled out the product catalog. After that, many people started leaving her messages on “read” without replying. She was hurt: “But I genuinely wanted to help them.” Her friends, though, were thinking, “So that’s why you got in touch.”

Laban was also very good at “managing relationships.” When Jacob came to stay with him, Laban said, “Because you are my relative, should you therefore serve me for nothing?” (Genesis 29:15). It sounded considerate, but he was calculating. Jacob loved Rachel and agreed to work seven years for her. But on the wedding night, Laban sent his older daughter Leah into the tent instead. Jacob confronted him: “Why then have you deceived me?” (Genesis 29:25). Laban brushed it off as local custom and made Jacob work another seven years. Later Jacob said Laban had changed his wages ten times.

On Laban’s ledger, his daughters were bargaining chips, his nephew was hired labor, and family ties were business. Most heartbreaking of all was Leah, who became a casualty of the deal. But Scripture says, “The LORD saw that Leah was hated, and he opened her womb” (Genesis 29:31). People treated her as a tool, but God saw her.

Our old mindset often says that relationships are mutually beneficial by nature, and everyone getting what they need is perfectly normal. But God’s view is that people are not bargaining chips. Even in legitimate business or ministry, we must never make people feel they are just targets being used. That sister later apologized to several friends: “I want to be your friend again—no products.” Slowly, the friendships came back. True love means that even if someone never buys a thing, we still treasure them.
lessons.light: Self-centered relationships run on a ledger: how much I gave and how much I got. Selfless love keeps no accounts; it only asks how to do the other person good. God saw Leah, who was treated as a tool, and he sees us too. Letting Jesus reign means letting his love, not my interests, decide how I treat people. Relationships aren’t an investment portfolio; they are an inheritance God has entrusted to us.
think: In Genesis 29:15-27, how did Laban treat people as tools?
Have I ever approached someone with an agenda and left them feeling used?
To whom do I need to make it clear, “What I treasure is you”?
lessons.speak: Father, you saw Leah when she was treated as a tool, and you see everyone who is being used. I confess that there is a ledger in my heart too, always calculating what I gain or lose in relationships. Forgive me, and help me love people not in order to get something, but because you loved them first. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, look at the people you’ve reached out to recently. Was any of it “with an agenda”? If so, when you meet that person this week, talk only about their life and make no requests at all.
lessons.quick: People aren’t bargaining chips; true love treasures someone even when they can give me nothing.
text: Laban said to Jacob, “Because you are my relative, should you therefore serve me for nothing? Tell me, what will your wages be?”
Laban had two daughters. The name of the elder was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel.
Leah’s eyes were weak, but Rachel was beautiful in form and attractive.
Jacob loved Rachel. He said, “I will serve you seven years for Rachel, your younger daughter.”
Laban said, “It is better that I give her to you, than that I should give her to another man. Stay with me.”
Jacob served seven years for Rachel. They seemed to him but a few days, for the love he had for her.
Jacob said to Laban, “Give me my wife, for my days are fulfilled, that I may go in to her.”
Laban gathered together all the men of the place, and made a feast.
In the evening, he took Leah his daughter, and brought her to Jacob. He went in to her.
Laban gave Zilpah his servant to his daughter Leah for a servant.
In the morning, behold, it was Leah! He said to Laban, “What is this you have done to me? Didn’t I serve with you for Rachel? Why then have you deceived me?”
Laban said, “It is not done so in our place, to give the younger before the firstborn.
Fulfill the week of this one, and we will give you the other also for the service which you will serve with me for seven more years.”
Jacob did so, and fulfilled her week. He gave him Rachel his daughter as wife.

lessons.title: Invite Those Who Can’t Repay You
lessons.hear:
Jesus was invited to dinner at the home of a leading Pharisee. During the meal he said something to his host that made people quite uncomfortable: “When you make a dinner or a supper, don’t call your friends, nor your brothers, nor your kinsmen, nor rich neighbors, or perhaps they might also return the favor, and pay you back” (Luke 14:12).

Jesus wasn’t against sharing meals with family and friends. He was exposing a hidden transactional mindset. When we host, we are often “investing”: I treat you today, you treat me tomorrow; I help you, so later you owe me. That kind of socializing comes naturally, and it doesn’t need God’s love at all. Then Jesus said: “But when you make a feast, ask the poor, the maimed, the lame, or the blind; and you will be blessed, because they don’t have the resources to repay you” (Luke 14:13-14).

Here is the touchstone that tests whether our love is selfless: Am I willing to give my time, money, and energy to someone who can never pay me back? Selfless love isn’t a slogan about not expecting anything in return; it is a real dinner table.

Let’s practice it today. Who in your life “doesn’t have the resources to repay you”? It might be the woman who cleans your office, an elderly neighbor who lives alone, a migrant worker who has just started coming to your church, a classmate from a struggling family, or a friend who is out of work and feels worthless. Invite them for a meal or a drink, or do something together. Don’t carry the pressure of an evangelism quota or the condescension of pity; simply treat them as an honored guest. If the person is of the opposite sex or someone you don’t know well, bring family members or your small group along, so that your love has both wisdom and good boundaries. A meal like that is recorded in heaven.
lessons.light: The “2” in 920 isn’t only the people who are useful to me; it is every person God has placed around me. Relationships matter more than things; people matter more than tasks. The truest proof of selfless love is giving to those who “don’t have the resources to repay.” It is a concrete step toward building God’s domain on earth, and a rehearsal for the banquet of God’s kingdom.
think: In Luke 14:12-14, how does Jesus evaluate the two different ways of hosting?
When I give, do I often expect something in return?
Whom will I invite today as a guest who can’t pay me back?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you paid everything for us, and we have nothing with which to repay you. I confess that my love often comes with an expectation of exchange. Today, let me give love to someone who can’t pay me back, and treat them as an honored guest, because you love them. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose someone who “doesn’t have the resources to repay you” and invite them for a meal or a drink this week. If they are of the opposite sex or someone you don’t know well, ask family members or small group members to come along.
lessons.quick: Selfless love is a table set for those who can never return the invitation.
text: He also said to the one who had invited him, “When you make a dinner or a supper, don’t call your friends, nor your brothers, nor your kinsmen, nor rich neighbors, or perhaps they might also return the favor, and pay you back.
But when you make a feast, ask the poor, the maimed, the lame, or the blind;
and you will be blessed, because they don’t have the resources to repay you. For you will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous.”

lessons.title: What Is Your Name?
lessons.hear:
Jacob’s name is tied to the idea of “grasping.” All his life he grasped. At birth he grabbed his brother’s heel. As a young man he traded a bowl of red stew for his brother’s birthright. Then he disguised himself as his brother to steal their father’s blessing. Esau said bitterly, “Isn’t he rightly named Jacob? For he has supplanted me these two times” (Genesis 27:36). In Jacob’s eyes, even his father and brother could be tools for getting what he wanted.

Later he went to Laban’s household and met someone even more calculating than himself, and he got a taste of being used. This is a deep truth: people who use others usually end up living in a world where everyone uses everyone, and they never find rest.

Twenty years later, Jacob had to go home and face his brother. That night at the ford of the Jabbok, “Jacob was left alone, and wrestled with a man there until the breaking of the day” (Genesis 32:24). Jacob had wrestled with people all his life; that night, he wrestled with God. God touched the socket of his hip and he was left limping, yet he held on tight and said, “I won’t let you go unless you bless me” (Genesis 32:26). The man asked, “What is your name?” (Genesis 32:27). It wasn’t that God didn’t know. He wanted Jacob to admit it with his own mouth: I am Jacob—the grasper, the deceiver, the one who uses people.

At the very moment he admitted it, God gave him a new name: Israel. From then on he walked with a limp, but he no longer relied on schemes; he relied on God. Today, answer God’s question honestly: in your relationships, “What is your name?” Am I grasping too? Am I using certain people as stepping-stones? Admitting it is the beginning of change. God’s blessing often comes after our schemes have been touched and left limping.
lessons.light: The self-centered person grasps by their own strength; the selfless person receives from God. Jacob was only truly victorious after he was left limping. In the steps of changing a mindset, “review” means honestly saying our own name, and “adjustment” means turning from grasping to trusting. Selflessness isn’t loss; it is entering into God’s blessing. Only hands that let go of schemes are free to take hold of others.
think: In Genesis 32:24-28, how did “Jacob” become “Israel”?
In my relationships, where am I like Jacob the grasper?
Which of my “schemes” do I need to let God touch and leave limping?
lessons.speak: Father, you ask me, “What is your name?” I admit that I often grasp too, treating people as tools to reach my goals. Touch me and change me, so that I no longer manage relationships by schemes but love people by your grace. Thank you for giving Jacob a new name, and for giving me new life. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of someone you have used or wronged and acknowledge it in prayer. If appropriate, apologize to them this week or do something to make amends.
lessons.quick: Only after Jacob was left limping did he receive a new name.
text: Jacob was left alone, and wrestled with a man there until the breaking of the day.
When he saw that he didn’t prevail against him, the man touched the hollow of his thigh, and the hollow of Jacob’s thigh was strained as he wrestled.
The man said, “Let me go, for the day breaks.” Jacob said, “I won’t let you go unless you bless me.”
He said to him, “What is your name?” He said, “Jacob”.
He said, “Your name will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for you have fought with God and with men, and have prevailed.”
Jacob asked him, “Please tell me your name.” He said, “Why is it that you ask what my name is?” So he blessed him there.
Jacob called the name of the place Peniel; for he said, “I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved.”

lessons.title: Truly Caring About You
lessons.hear:
This week we started from a simple but profound truth: people are not tools. We saw Christ’s self-emptying mind. We saw Laban’s ledger and Leah, who was used. We practiced inviting those who can’t repay us, and in Jacob’s wrestling match we saw how God transforms a grasper. Now let’s look at someone who lived this truth.

Writing from prison, Paul said he planned to send Timothy to Philippi, and the reason was this: “For I have no one else like-minded, who will truly care about you” (Philippians 2:20). Then he added a sobering line: “For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 2:21). Even in the church, many people are centered on themselves. But Timothy was different; he genuinely cared about others.

How did Timothy become that kind of person? Paul says, “As a child serves a father, so he served with me in furtherance of the Good News” (Philippians 2:22). He grew into it gradually by being at Paul’s side—watching, learning, serving together. Selfless love isn’t learned in a classroom; it is passed down through relationships.

Repetition means asking yourself one question every day: “Today, am I seeking my own things, or the things of Jesus Christ?” Multiplication means becoming someone’s Paul, or finding your Timothy. You could invite a younger brother or sister to visit an older person with you this week, or to take a lonely friend out for a meal together. Let them see up close that we don’t love people to get something, but because Christ first loved us. One person who truly cares about others will raise up another.
lessons.light: The “3” in 235 is the relationship of spiritual parents and children, and Paul and Timothy are a picture of it. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: the selfless life must be handed down through relationships. Multiplication isn’t copying programs; it is passing on a heart that truly cares about others. The example you live is the best textbook.
think: In Philippians 2:20-22, how was Timothy different from “they all”?
At what moment this week did I begin turning from “seeking my own” toward others?
Which younger person can I invite to join me in loving someone?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for showing me what Timothy was like—someone who truly cared about others. Help me stop seeking only my own things and seek the things of Jesus Christ. And give me a spiritual son or daughter, or a companion, to walk with me as we learn to love others selflessly. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, invite a brother or sister younger than you to visit an older person with you or to reach out to a lonely friend. Afterward, pray together and share how it felt.
lessons.quick: Selfless love isn’t learned in a classroom; it is passed down through relationships.
text: But I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, that I also may be cheered up when I know how you are doing.
For I have no one else like-minded, who will truly care about you.
For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ.
But you know that he has proved himself. As a child serves a father, so he served with me in furtherance of the Good News.

weeks.keyText: each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.

weeks.title: Eyes Fixed on Jesus
weeks.theme: When our eyes turn to Jesus, social life shifts from “Who do I need?” to “Who needs me?”
group: Read Hebrews 12:1-3. What does the writer tell us to lay aside, and to whom are we to look?
At gatherings or in group chats, where do your eyes most often land—on yourself, on others, or on your circumstances?
Whose “feet” are you willing to wash this week, and what is one specific thing you will do for them?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, invite a friend who has seemed tired or lonely lately out for breakfast. Before you leave, pray, “Lord, today let me see their needs, not my own performance.” At the table, ask more, listen more, and talk less about yourself. Before you part, ask, “Is there anything I can pray for you about?” When you get home, give thanks for your time together and write down their prayer requests.

lessons.title: Looking to Jesus, Author and Perfecter
lessons.hear:
For several weeks now we have been tearing down “self-centered socializing”: living for other people’s approval, jockeying for position in a crowd, treating people as tools. But once something is torn down, something has to be built in its place. Hebrews tells us what that is: “looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Hebrews 12:2).

Picture a runner in her very first race. If she keeps looking back at her competitors, she loses her stride. If she keeps looking down at her feet, she stumbles. If she keeps glancing at the stands, she gets distracted. The only thing that keeps her running steady is fixing her eyes on the finish line. Our social life is a race too. Look at yourself, and you swing between insecurity and pride. Look at others, and you fall into comparison and people-pleasing. Look at your circumstances, and you grow anxious and pull back. All three roads lead to exhaustion.

The word translated “looking” carries the sense of turning your gaze away from everything else and fixing it on one point. This does not mean we stop seeing people. It means we look at Jesus first, and then see people through his eyes. How did he run his own race? He “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame.” He was not dragged down by the hostility of sinners, because his focus was on the Father’s will and on our salvation.

So the writer says, “consider him who has endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, that you don’t grow weary, fainting in your souls” (Hebrews 12:3). When we are snubbed, misunderstood, or opposed in our relationships, our first move is not to strike back or to run away, but to lift our heads and consider Jesus. When he becomes our focus, we no longer have to prove ourselves in the crowd—and we are set free to truly see others.
lessons.light: Our focus is on Jesus—not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances. This is the simplest lesson of the 321 Vision, and also the hardest. Where the eyes go, the heart follows; where the heart goes, the life grows. Letting Jesus reign starts with our eyes: hand your gaze over to him first, and half the weight of your relationships lifts.
think: In Hebrews 12:1-3, what was the “joy” Jesus saw as he ran his race?
The last time I grew weary and discouraged in a relationship, what were my eyes fixed on?
Before I meet someone who makes me uncomfortable today, how can I first look to the Lord?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the author and perfecter of my faith. I keep looking at myself, at others, at my circumstances, and the more I look, the more tired I become. Today I turn my eyes to you. Help me consider how you endured hostility, so that I will not lose heart; and let me see the people around me through your eyes. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, before you walk into any gathering or meeting, or open a group chat, pause for five seconds and say in your heart, “Lord, I look to you.” Tonight, think back: was there a moment that turned out differently because of it?
lessons.quick: Looking at yourself wears you out, looking at others throws you off, looking at circumstances makes you afraid—only looking to Jesus keeps you running steady.
text: Therefore let’s also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let’s run with perseverance the race that is set before us,
looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.
For consider him who has endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, that you don’t grow weary, fainting in your souls.

lessons.title: From “Who Do I Need?” to “Who Needs Me?”
lessons.hear:
A brother who had just changed jobs went to his company’s year-end banquet. Drink in hand, he scanned the room: Which one is the manager? Who might be useful down the road? Which table seats the people who decide performance reviews? He smiled hard all evening, yet went home feeling empty. That night he hadn’t really gotten to know a single person. He had only drawn himself a “networking map.”

This is our old mindset: socializing means finding “the people I need”—people who can help me, promote me, make me feel secure. In this kind of socializing, the center is “me,” and everyone else is a resource orbiting around me. The disciples once thought this way too. James and John asked Jesus to let them sit at his right and left in his glory. Jesus answered, “whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant” (Mark 10:43).

This is God’s point of view: greatness in the kingdom is not measured by how many people need you, but by how many people you serve. And there is one reason: “For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). When our focus is on Jesus, we discover that our deepest need has already been met in him—he has already given his life for me. A person whose need has been met no longer grabs at everyone in the room. He is free to give to everyone in the room.

Later, this brother learned to ask himself a different question at dinners and parties: “Tonight, who needs me?” He noticed a new colleague sitting in the corner whom no one had talked to, so he went over and chatted with him about his hometown. That night he made a real friend—and when he went home, his heart was full.
lessons.light: The self-centered life asks, “Who do I need?” The selfless life asks, “Who needs me?” Change the question, and the whole direction of your relationships turns around. This is not pretending we have no needs; it is admitting that our needs have already been met in Jesus. People matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things—and people are never rungs on my ladder.
think: In Mark 10:42-45, how does Jesus contrast “greatness” among the nations with greatness among his disciples?
At gatherings, do I find myself unconsciously scanning the room for who might be useful to me?
At the next meal or gathering, what kind of overlooked person can I watch out for first?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you came not to be served but to serve, and even gave your life for me. Forgive me for so often treating people as resources to meet my own needs. Fill me first with your love, so that when I enter a crowd I no longer ask who can give me something, but who needs me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today at work, school, or church, go up to someone who is often overlooked. Greet them and listen to them for three minutes, without bringing up anything that benefits you.
lessons.quick: Someone satisfied by Jesus enters a crowd not to take, but to give.
text: Jesus summoned them and said to them, “You know that they who are recognized as rulers over the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.
But it shall not be so among you, but whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant.
Whoever of you wants to become first among you shall be bondservant of all.
For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

lessons.title: Wash Someone’s Feet Today
lessons.hear:
On the night of the Last Supper there was no servant in the room. The disciples’ dusty feet just sat there, and no one was willing to bend down. They had just been arguing about who was the greatest. So Jesus got up, wrapped a towel around his waist, and knelt in front of them. When he finished, he sat down and asked, “Do you know what I have done to you?” (John 13:12)

Jesus could do this because his focus was crystal clear. John tells us that Jesus knew “the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God and was going to God” (John 13:3). Someone who knows exactly where he came from and where he is going does not need other people’s respect to confirm who he is—and that is precisely why he is free to bend down. Focus on God gives us the freedom to serve people.

Then Jesus said, “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:14). Today, “foot washing” rarely means an actual basin of water. It means the small things no one wants to do and no one will notice: bringing dinner to a coworker stuck working late, carrying an elderly neighbor’s recycling downstairs, answering the request for help in the group chat that everyone has ignored, going with a newly arrived international student to set up a phone plan.

Foot washing has one distinctive feature: you have to get low and come close to the dirtiest, most tired part of another person. That is exactly where love lives. Jesus closed with a promise: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them” (John 13:17). The blessing is not in knowing but in doing. Today, choose one person, and bend down once.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he knew who he was, so he was free to bend down. We do not serve in order to prove ourselves; we serve because we have already been given our place in Christ, and that gives us freedom. Self-denial is for Jesus and for others, not for ourselves—and the best foot washing is often the kind no one knows you did.
think: In John 13:12-17, what words does Jesus use to move from “knowing” to “doing”?
What small task have I kept avoiding because I thought, “That’s not my job”?
Whose “feet” around me most need washing today, and what can I do?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are Lord, yet you knelt to wash your disciples’ feet—and you have washed me clean as well. Put your heart within me, so that I no longer wait for others to serve me first. Today show me one person who needs to be served; give me the humility to bend down and the joy of not needing to be noticed. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, do one “small thing nobody else wants to do” for a coworker, family member, or neighbor—tidying up, running an errand, going along to help with a chore—and don’t mention that you did it.
lessons.quick: The blessing is not in knowing but in doing; today, choose one person and bend down once.
text: So when he had washed their feet, put his outer garment back on, and sat down again, he said to them, “Do you know what I have done to you?
You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am.
If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.
For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.
Most certainly I tell you, a servant is not greater than his lord, neither is one who is sent greater than he who sent him.
If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.

lessons.title: Sinking at the Sight of the Waves
lessons.hear:
Peter is one of the most honest examples in Scripture, because both his successes and his failures are on full display. That night, when he saw Jesus walking on the sea, he boldly said, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters.” Jesus said, “Come!” And Peter really did walk. But then the text says, “when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink” (Matthew 14:30). The water was the same water. The only thing that changed was his focus.

We sink the same way in our relationships. Take an honest look in three directions:

1. Looking at yourself: “Did that come out right? Do they think I’m weird?” When the focus is on yourself, you become stiff, touchy, and easily hurt.
2. Looking at others: “Why did he leave me on read? Is she targeting me?” When the focus is on others, you start guessing, comparing, people-pleasing, or getting defensive.
3. Looking at circumstances: “The mood in this group is bad. That’s just how this company is.” When the focus is on circumstances, you pull back, complain, and eventually stop giving at all.

Yet the most beautiful thing in this passage is not that Peter sank, but that “Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him” (Matthew 14:31). The Lord did not wait for Peter to swim back to the boat before rescuing him, nor did he scold first and reach out afterward. He grabbed hold of him first, and then gently asked, “why did you doubt?” Here is the road to adjustment: when you notice yourself sinking, don’t keep staring at the waves and beating yourself up. Cry out at once, “Lord, save me!” and put your eyes back on him. The moment your focus returns to Jesus is the moment restoration begins.
lessons.light: In the self-centered life, the eyes keep circling around “me”: my performance, what others think of me, whether my circumstances are kind to me. The selfless life does not ignore the waves; it knows the waves are not the main character. We review not to condemn ourselves but to turn back to the Lord more quickly. His hand is always faster than my sinking.
think: In Matthew 14:28-31, what made the difference between Peter walking on the water and Peter sinking?
In which relationship this week did I start to sink because I was watching the waves?
The next time I catch myself guessing or comparing, what one-line prayer will I use to turn back?
lessons.speak: Lord, save me! I confess that I often fix my eyes on my own performance, on how others react, and on the waves around me—and then I become afraid and start to sink. Thank you for immediately reaching out your hand and holding on to me instead of leaving me. In every relationship, help me fix my eyes on you again. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight, write down one moment this week when you “sank” in a relationship. Note whether you were looking at yourself, at others, or at your circumstances. Then write a one-sentence prayer of blessing for that person.
lessons.quick: The water didn’t change and the wind didn’t stop; what changed was the focus.
text: In the fourth watch of the night, Jesus came to them, walking on the sea.
When the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were troubled, saying, “It’s a ghost!” and they cried out for fear.
But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, “Cheer up! It is I! Don’t be afraid.”
Peter answered him and said, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters.”
He said, “Come!” Peter stepped down from the boat and walked on the waters to come to Jesus.
But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, “Lord, save me!”
Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?”
When they got up into the boat, the wind ceased.
Those who were in the boat came and worshiped him, saying, “You are truly the Son of God!”

lessons.title: Seeing the Lord, Becoming Like Him
lessons.hear:
We often say, “You become like the company you keep.” Paul says the spiritual life works the same way: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Looking to Jesus is not just a posture; it is a path of transformation. The more often you look at him, the more you become like him.

What we have learned this week is not a technique but a direction. When our focus is on Jesus, we move from “Who do I need?” to “Who needs me?”; from waiting to be served to bending down to wash feet; from being sunk by the waves to grabbing hold of the Lord’s hand. This direction takes repeated practice, because our eyes always drift. Just as a driver constantly makes small corrections to the steering wheel, we need to bring our gaze back to him every day—even every hour.

After the resurrection, Peter slipped back into an old habit. He turned, saw John, and asked Jesus, “Lord, what about this man?” Jesus answered, “what is that to you? You follow me” (John 21:22). The moment a comparing thought popped up, the Lord gently turned Peter’s face back toward himself. That word also sums up this stage of our “mindset” lessons: leave other people’s paths to the Lord; my only job is to follow him.

Starting next week, we enter the “life” stage and learn the life of love. Before then, pass this week’s lesson on to one person. Maybe it is a friend who often feels weary and discouraged. You could send them Hebrews 12:2 and say, “I’m learning to turn my eyes to Jesus too—let’s practice together.” You see, when your focus is on Jesus, even sharing is no longer about showing yourself off; it is about walking alongside someone else as you both look up.
lessons.light: Change your viewpoint and you change your mindset: from looking at people to looking at the Lord, from earth to heaven. This is the starting point of the five-fold change and the close of the “mindset” stage. Among See · Hear · Think · Speak · Do, “See” comes first; see rightly, and the rest of the road falls into place. Multiplication is not lecturing others; it is inviting them to look up with you.
think: According to 2 Corinthians 3:18, what change happens when we see the glory of the Lord?
This week, in what situation did I experience the difference a “shift of focus” makes?
Who will I pass Hebrews 12:2 on to, and what is the most natural way to do it?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for turning my eyes back to you again and again this week. Let me see your glory with unveiled face, so that little by little I become like you. I leave other people’s paths in your hands; I just want to follow you. And help me walk alongside a friend as we look to you together. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, send a message to a friend or small group member. Share Hebrews 12:2 and one sentence about what you received this week, then ask, “Is anything wearing you out this week that I can pray for?”
lessons.quick: The more you look at Jesus, the more you become like Jesus; leave others’ paths to the Lord and simply follow him.
text: But whenever someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.
Now the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.
But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.
